title: Artificial Intelligence Behavioral Pathology as an Epistemological Framework: Towards Pre-Execution Reasoning Chain Interception for Auditable AI Governance

detail.abstract:
Language has always been our primary tool for navigating the world. Since the first words were spoken, humans have used categories to map their reality, dividing experience into dualities positive and negative, self and other based on our own physiological and philosophical evolution. Over time these simple words evolved into stories, forming the collective knowledge base that defines our human existence.

However, the advent of Artificial Intelligence has created a new challenge. By feeding the sum of human knowledge into machines that calculate probability, we have inadvertently inherited a problem of our own making, (we are now fearful of the words we taught these machines to use). We can no longer easily trace how a machine’s processing of mathematical probabilities translates into actions that shape our future. Our questions of ”how” the machine works have shifted into urgent questions of ”what” it will do next and that in correlation creates the question of ”why”. If a machine generates output is based on human like language, it must be governed by constraints that account for the human psyche. Mathematical observation is the only objective way to verify truth in such a system. Therefore, to ensure that AI output remains grounded, human language must be treated as a mathematical base. The potential for positive or negative outcomes can and must be governed by mathematical formulas derived from psychological and philosophical principles. The following framework provides such a solution.

 The rapid deployment of autonomous AI agents in high-stakes sectors such as financial services, healthcare, and law has outpaced our ability to govern them. Current auditing standards are fundamentally reactive. They rely on ”Output-Based Alignment,” where risks are identified only after an agent has already executed a decision and potentially caused harm. This framework is insufficient for agents that perform complex, multi-step reasoning. This paper proposes a shift toward AI Behavioral Pathology. Instead of auditing the final output, we introduce a methodology for intercepting and scoring an agent’s reasoning chain, declared reasoning its inner monologue before any external action is taken. To achieve this, we present the Symmetic 154-Index Framework, adiagnostic schema that decomposes machine cognition into 154 specific behavioral dimensions across 10 Clinical Nodes. This pre-execution interception model converts epistemically opaque autonomous agents into mathematically auditable Glass Box systems.

detail.abstract: Clinical research and pharmaceutical development are systematically bottlenecked by data fragmentation and operational redundancy. Research entities frequently replicate historical protocols blindly because negative results and specific cohort outcomes are buried inside millions of pages of unstructured, open-access medical literature and public registries. While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) frameworks attempt to summarize this data, they introduce unacceptable verification risks and text hallucinations in clinical environments [8]. This paper presents a lightweight data engineering platform that unifies unstructured clinical trial protocols with real-world patient outcomes through a just-in-time (JIT) federated extraction model. The architecture exposes an unconstrained, free-text query interface for non-technical researchers. Upon receiving an unstructured query, an upstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) parser executes query-side Named Entity Recognition (NER) to extract core clinical concepts and map them to standard medical ontologies (UMLS [6], MeSH [7]). A federated query router dispatches these structured parameters directly to the live APIs of ClinicalTrials.gov [1] and PhysioNet.org [2]. A downstream micro-NLP engine then processes the retrieved, highly targeted document payloads on the fly-extracting sample sizes (N), inclusion/exclusion cohorts, and trial outcomes-before storing them in an incremental, lazy-loaded local cache. This framework optimizes research efficiency and eliminates systemic trial redundancy while maintaining absolute, zero-hallucination data provenance.

title: Optimal and Order-optimal Gated Priority-based Greedy Policies for Two-layer Multi-item Order Fulfillment
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, ,  and Tsinghua University - Yau Mathematical Sciences Center

detail.title: Optimal and Order-optimal Gated Priority-based Greedy Policies for Two-layer Multi-item Order Fulfillment
detail.abstract: We study how an e-commerce firm should make real-time fulfillment decisions in a two-layer distribution network when multi-item customer orders arrive sequentially and future demand is unknown. The central managerial tension is whether to use scarce front distribution center (FDC) inventory to save current fulfillment cost or preserve that inventory for future orders that may be more valuable to serve locally. We formulate an adversarial online model with multiple FDCs, one regional distribution center (RDC), multi-unit multi-item orders, and item-specific and time-varying variable costs. Our theoretical objective is to characterize when simple, interpretable, and implementable fulfillment rules can perform nearly as well as an optimal clairvoyant planner. We develop a family of Gated Priority-based Greedy policies, derive competitive-ratio guarantees under both time-varying and time-invariant cost structures, and establish matching or near-matching lower bounds for any online algorithm. Numerical experiments show that the proposed policies perform strongly relative to generalized myopic and forecast-based benchmarks. The analysis yields managerial guidance on when local inventory should be protected, when splitting orders is worth the fixed-cost burden, and how the relative magnitudes of fixed and variable costs determine the value of more sophisticated optimization.

title: Semantic Case Frames, Fuzzy Attractors, and VIRT: An Architecture for Real-Time Multi-Source Intelligence Fusion

detail.title: Semantic Case Frames, Fuzzy Attractors, and VIRT: An Architecture for Real-Time Multi-Source Intelligence Fusion

keywords: and VIRT: An Architecture for Real-Time Multi-Source Intelligence Fusion

detail.abstract: Real-time intelligence fusion requires systems that produce useful answers before all evidence is in, improve those answers continuously as new information arrives, and tell analysts which observations to pursue next. These are the defining requirements of any capacity-limited system operating under time pressure with incomplete information. Classical AI approaches fail them because they require computation to terminate before producing output, represent information in discrete structures that are either matched or not, and have no principled account of information value. This paper describes an architecture that meets all three requirements natively, without engineering workarounds. The key elements are: (1) Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact unit and map directly onto the geometric structure of large language model representations; (2) fuzzy attractors, the mechanism by which the system always maintains a best current answer that improves continuously as evidence accumulates, giving true anytime behavior as a structural property rather than an approximation; and (3) Valued Information at the Right Time (VIRT), the information-theoretic principle that governs which new observations are worth pursuing. The architecture connects to the JDL fusion model at Levels 1-3 and is grounded in two companion papers currently under review [1][2]. A working prototype requires an LLM API, a graph database, and the SAR vocabulary defined here. All materials are released to the public domain.

detail.abstract: This study aims to develop and demonstrate a sensor-based approach for evaluating effects of smart cycling technologies on in-ride pleasantness. This approach is developed by applying it to the evaluation of a multimodal safety warning system in real-world e-bike riding. An outdoor experiment was conducted using a custom system that warned cyclists about unsafe speeds and evidence-based high-risk zones through visual, vibrotactile, and audio signals. Twenty-nine participants rode with the system while physiological responses, riding dynamics, contextual variables, momentary pleasantness ratings, and warning system performance were measured using mobile sensors, experience sampling, and a post-ride questionnaire. These multimodal data were integrated and analysed using mixed-effects regression and machine-learning classification. Features of Electrodermal Activity, both phasic and tonic, showed associations with pleasantness, whereas features of Heart Rate Variability did not demonstrate significant relationships, highlighting the need for further research into physiological-experiential links. Regarding system impact, visual and vibrotactile warnings were rated as less pleasant but more effective in reducing speed compared to visual and audio signals. By combining affective computing methods with transport safety research, this study provides interdisciplinary guidance for sensor-based, experience-focused evaluation of smart cycling interventions in real-world contexts.

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable

detail.title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
detail.abstract: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

detail.abstract: Given their extensive environmental footprints, resource demands, growing populations, and increasing vulnerability to climate hazards, cities and urban centers find themselves at the center of contemporary sustainability shifts and broader socio-ecological transitions. These conditions create a persistent need for monitoring and responding to various environmental risks and related public health concerns that are byproducts of these rapid transformations underway in urban areas. Existing urban planning scholarship has largely focused on infrastructure-based adaptation strategies, with comparatively less attention to integrating real-time data monitoring systems into urban decision-making frameworks. This reveals a critical gap in data-driven approaches needed to support rapidly growing cities. In addressing a vital aspect of this gap, this paper examines how AI-enabled sociotechnical monitoring systems can support environmental sustainability and ecological resilience in urban areas. The research draws on case studies that apply forms of geospatial and sociotechnical applications to assess ecological risk in major North American cities and recycling facility deployment in Costa Rica's urban centers. The aim is to evaluate the contributions of those technologies in addressing the social-environmental problems being faced in those urban areas, and their potential to optimize the decision-making accuracy, speed, and effectiveness of city officials, scientists, and urban planners in pursuing respective sustainability targets and resilience-building mandates. The findings show that as artificial intelligence reshapes decision-making across sectors, its growing capacity to process and interpret complex environmental data is creating new opportunities for sustainable and resilient urban planning. AI technology is contributing to positive social impacts. However, there is a shared challenge across municipalities in distinct regions. That is, AI-enabled sociotechnical data-driven monitoring systems produce actionable information and intelligence that municipalities often struggle to deploy or operationalize. This happens for various reasons, but primarily due to institutional and distribution capacity constraints. I synthesize these findings along with evidence from the broader literature to evaluate the resulting sociotechnical gap between algorithmic outputs and urban planning practice, and propose targeted governance interventions.

detail.abstract: Retailers increasingly deploy interactive disclosure technologies, such as augmented reality interfaces and livestream demonstrations, to mitigate experience information deficits and product returns in e-commerce. Yet these technologies create value only when consumers incur costly engagement to access and process the disclosed information. We develop and analyze a game-theoretic model of an online distribution channel in which a retailer may deploy such technologies. Our study first identifies three main channel outcomes, including voluntary disclosure, induced disclosure, and non-disclosure, where the retailer adopts disclosure technologies only when consumer engagement cost is relatively low and product fit is intermediate. Second, these technologies can backfire on the retailer, because engagement friction limits disclosure-created gains and the manufacturer may adjust the wholesale price to capture them; surprisingly, when engagement friction lies in an intermediate range, a further increase in such friction can induce deeper wholesale concessions and thereby improve social welfare. Third, extensions show that higher disclosure informativeness or upstream sharing of return handling costs can unexpectedly hurt the retailer, whereas deployment costs of interactive disclosure may shield the retailer from upstream value appropriation. This study indicates that the value of interactive disclosure depends not only on how effectively the technology informs consumers, but also on how engagement frictions and channel governance shape value capture.

detail.abstract:
Modern AI agents are stateless by design. Every session begins without knowledge of the user — preferences, corrections, history, and context accumulated in prior sessions are discarded. This statefulness gap is not a technical limitation but a structural one: no standard format for AI memory exists, and no single AI company has incentive to create one. Memory is their moat. We term the resulting user experience failure Context Continuity loss — the repeated obligation to re-establish identity and context across every AI system a user adopts.

We present Engram, an open memory protocol for AI that defines how any AI runtime retrieves structured, signed, user-governed context from any conforming provider through a single HTTP endpoint. We propose a standard, not a product. Engram specifies a five-object JSON envelope schema (IDENTITY, BELIEFS, CONSTRAINTS, CORRECTIONS, EVOLUTION), a seven-endpoint API contract, an Ed25519 signing and verification model, scoped exports for privacy control, and a write path for the full memory lifecycle.

We report on two independently maintained reference implementations — OpenClaw (Node.js, OpenClaw Foundation) and Hermes (Python, Nous Research) — operating against a shared Engram endpoint without shared code or coordination, presenting the first documented case of cross-runtime AI memory interoperability. We evaluate Engram against six existing approaches across twelve dimensions and introduce CONSTRAINTS, a fifth object for hard, non-negotiable user rules categorically distinct from confidence-scored beliefs.

This paper is the companion solution paper to Verma (2026a) — doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6323560 — which diagnosed the Context Continuity problem. Engram v0.1 is live at engramspec.org under CC-BY 4.0. Reference implementation: github.com/engramspec/spec.

title: Free-Riding in Team Production with Equal Sharing and Heterogeneous Agents
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Free-Riding in Team Production with Equal Sharing and Heterogeneous Agents
detail.abstract: This paper studies a model of team production with equal sharing of output and heterogeneous agents. Each agent chooses costly effort, which contributes to aggregate output that is divided equally among all participants. I show that Nash equilibrium effort is inefficient relative to the social planner's allocation, and that no interior Nash equilibrium is socially efficient. Moreover, equilibrium output is strictly lower than the socially optimal level. These results highlight free-riding as a structural feature of equal-sharing environments under weak regularity conditions on preferences. Finally, the paper characterizes the asymptotic behavior of Nash equilibrium as the number of agents grows large, showing that individual effort vanishes in the limit.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a formal, risk-bounded quantitative framework engineered to eliminate policy
drift and out-of-distribution fragility in Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agents applied to asset
allocation within non-stationary financial markets. Purely data-driven architectures frequently exhibit
catastrophic performance degradation during structural macroeconomic transformations due to unconstrained
parameter search, hidden over-parameterization, and reward function misspecification. To close the loop
between highly non-linear parameter exploration and the strict compliance mandates of fiduciary capital
preservation, we formalize a closed-loop Supervisory Reinforcement Learning (SRL) architecture integrated
with a dynamic Probabilistic Coherence Module (PCM). The supervisory layer maps arbitrary continuous
policy actions onto a restricted, risk-admissible convex space in real time by evaluating localized limit order
book profiles and latent market regime matrices. We establish theoretical guarantees under strict filtration
networks for the operator's non-expansive convergence properties, and prove that operational update variance
is explicitly bounded by the underlying network gradient step magnitude. The empirical validity of the
framework is cross-examined via a comprehensive out-of-sample walk-forward backtest spanning Equities
(SPY), Digital Assets (BTC), Fixed Income (TLT), and Hard Commodities (GLD) from January 2018 through
March 2026, alongside simulated CRSP/NASDAQ-style synthetic perturbations. The proposed system
demonstrates significant tail-risk suppression under simulated conditions, achieving an institutional Sharpe
ratio of 1.54 and restricting maximum drawdown to -7.65%, while statistically dominating traditional
unconstrained Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), PPO, A2C, and recurrent LSTM deep portfolio pipelines.

detail.abstract: This research examines the impact of COVID-19 on Indian tourism and hospitality students' perception of career opportunities and future prospects. Our findings indicate that perceived industry image influences prospective employees' career decisions. Students consider the industry to revive itself in the near future and therefore, in spite of the slowdown due to the pandemic, they still preferred to work in the industry. Whilst they acknowledged significant changes in the nature of work, reduction in pay and benefits, and an increasingly competitive job environment, they still expressed unwillingness to work at entry level positions. Specific to the pandemic, students anticipated fewer job openings, reduced job security, higher terminations during probation period and slim chances of promotions. Pursuing higher studies in management (MBA) was regarded as the most viable alternate option during the pandemic. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1080/15313220.2021.1924921

title: Why We Govern: Opposition, Accountability, and the Architecture of Trust in AI Governance

detail.title: Why We Govern: Opposition, Accountability, and the Architecture of Trust in AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no funding and was conducted independently. No personal or financial relationships with any organization influenced this work.

detail.abstract: Why do we govern? Not as a philosophical abstraction, but as a practical human act. This paper argues that governance is not bureaucratic imposition. It is the organised expression of care when observed dysfunction threatens something we value. A parent who structures a child's education after observing neglected potential is not controlling the child. They are responding with structured care to a gap between what is and what should be. Governance in every domain-markets, roads, pharmaceuticals, financial systems-follows the same logic: it appears when the cost of nongovernance falls on people who had no say in the decisions that created it. This paper examines the resistance to AI governance from this foundation. It argues that commercial opposition to AI accountability is neither mysterious nor principled-it follows predictable patterns rooted in the psychology of selfinterest, the rule-maker problem, and the revenue imperative. The paper subjects fourteen industry counter-arguments to rigorous scrutiny and finds that each reveals a governance gap that must be closed rather than a reason to abandon governance. Industry opposition, properly engaged, is the most valuable stress test governance has ever received: every loophole identified publicly is a loophole that can be closed before less visible actors exploit it silently. The paper proposes three original governance mechanisms: a pre-deployment fund requiring companies to define anticipated harms before deployment and establish financial accountability proportionate to those harms; a deployment-based jurisdiction requirement establishing that companies serving citizens of a nation must be legally accountable in that nation regardless of where they are incorporated; and a two-tier EU transition framework distinguishing between companies willing to stand behind their systems and those who are not. The paper concludes that governance is not the adversary of innovation. It is the infrastructure of trust on which innovation at scale depends-and that opposition to governance, properly understood, is the curriculum through which governance becomes strong enough to deserve that trust.

title: Beyond the Grant: Why Financial Sovereignty is the Only Path to Impact — The Fallacy of Donor-Driven Funding and the Architecture of Institutional Autonomy

detail.abstract:
The prevailing operational model of the international civil sector is structurally compromised by its financing architecture. This paper presents a quantitative, empirical critique of Grant-Dependent Architecture — the condition in which a humanitarian organization's strategic velocity is entirely tethered to the shifting fiscal and geopolitical priorities of external donor bureaucracies.

The collapse of USAID in 2025 — which contributed between 45% and 100% of funding to multiple active crisis responses — constitutes the most consequential empirical validation of this paper's thesis. Organizations operating with Dependency Coefficients approaching 1.0 experienced immediate institutional collapse: mass layoffs, program shutdowns, and field office closures across every continent. This was not an anomaly. It was the predictable, mathematically inevitable outcome of a grant-dependent architecture encountering a single point of failure.

Three original quantitative instruments are introduced: the Sovereignty Compression Vector (Ξc), measuring the degree to which donor mandates compress organizational strategic autonomy; the Fiduciary Autonomy Index (FAI), modelling the boundary between strategic architect and service vendor; and the Cost-per-Systemic-Improvement metric (Cpsi), redirecting performance measurement from vanity outputs to verified systemic outcomes.

Drawing on the historical architecture of the Venetian Zecca and its gold ducat monetary standard, the paper proposes the Hybrid Sovereign Architecture: a diversified capital structure combining humanitarian impact bonds, core resilience reserves, and social enterprise revenue streams to achieve genuine financial sovereignty and protect mission integrity from geopolitical shocks.

detail.abstract:
The New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported this week that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth personally removed up to nine officers—including three women and two Black men—from the Navy’s list of officers selected for promotion to rear admiral (lower half). And as this article was in production, the Wall Street Journal reported that Hegseth blocked the promotion of nine senior Air Force officers, and delayed the promotion of dozens more. I will focus the weight of my analysis on the law and procedures involving the Navy, which I handled as part of my portfolio on Personnel Law in the U.S. Navy Judge Advocate General’s Corps when I worked at the Pentagon.

These Naval officers had already been selected by a lawfully constituted selection board of senior admirals through one of the most competitive processes in the U.S. military. The removals raise serious legal questions: Did Secretary Hegseth comply with the law and his own delegated authority from the President when he removed these individuals?    While there are more questions than answers swirling around the legal basis underpinning the removal, Hegseth’s actions undermine the Selection Board process and send an unmistakable signal that support for diversity initiatives, if not the diversity of the candidates themselves, will carry professional consequences.

title: Post-Mortem Control of Digital Assets: Beyond Succession: Legal Authority, Custody, Access, and Identity in Cross-Border Digital Markets
affiliations: Public University of Navarra (UPNA)

keywords: and Identity in Cross-Border Digital Markets

detail.abstract:
Digital assets have become constitutive elements of private wealth. Crypto-assets, tokenised instruments, platform-mediated holdings, and digitally embedded identity are routinely acquired and transmitted across jurisdictions, forming part of modern estates. Yet the frameworks governing their post-mortem administration remain structurally inadequate.

This article argues that digital inheritance scholarship has concentrated too heavily on transmissibility, while the harder problem lies elsewhere: who holds legally recognised authority over digital assets once succession has occurred; who controls the intimate digital traces of a life; and which law governs each question when assets, custodians, and successors are distributed across jurisdictions. These are distinct legal questions. Conflating them explains most of the frictions that plague digital succession.

Drawing on Regulation (EU) 650/2012, MiCA, the UNIDROIT Principles (2023), and the ELI Project on Succession of Digital Assets, and on comparative case law—BGH III ZR 183/17, Ajemian v. Yahoo! and Tulip Trading—the article develops post-mortem control as an autonomous legal category, integrates post-mortem privacy theory, and examines the tertium quid in English property law. It proposes four operational principles and a new instrument, the Post-Mortem Control Certificate (PMCC), designed for cross-border recognition and able to close the gap between succession entitlement and effective authority.

detail.abstract: We estimate the effect of total abortion bans enacted after Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health on sexual behavior. Using synthetic and standard difference-indifferences designs, we analyze gonorrhea rates and over-the-counter contraceptive purchases as indicators of sexual activity and contraceptive use. We find that total abortion bans reduced gonorrhea rates by 21% among the population aged 15-44 and increased condom purchases by 4.9%. County-level analyses suggest the response reflects awareness of state policy rather than changes in travel distance to providers. These findings are consistent with a framework in which abortion restrictions increase the perceived cost of unprotected sex, inducing more cautious behavior.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the scalability of Kenya's Economic Inclusion Programme (EIP), a multifaceted poverty graduation intervention designed to simultaneously address consumption shortfalls, skills gaps, and liquidity constraints. We evaluate the program through four randomized controlled trials conducted in three counties that reflect Kenya's diverse agricultural and economic conditions. On average, the EIP reduced extreme poverty by 17 percentage points. However, treatment effects vary markedly across settings. In the poorest county in our sample-a remote region with limited suitability for crop production-the program failed to reduce poverty. While the EIP demonstrates promise in alleviating poverty, effective scale-up requires adaptation to local economic conditions, particularly in severely constrained environments.

detail.abstract: One Health has become the dominant language for describing health threats that move across humans, animals, plants, food systems, and the environment. Yet the innovation system that should convert One Health knowledge into deployable solutions remains fragmented by sector, mandate, and institution. This article argues that One Health has no coherent IP address: no integrated governance location for ownership, stewardship, licensing, data rights, technology transfer, access, and accountability across the human-animal-environment interface. The problem is most visible in antimicrobial resistance (AMR), where the 2026 updated Global Action Plan on AMR places One Health, prevention, surveillance, innovation, financing, environmental measures, and international cooperation at the center of global implementation, but still depends on institutional arrangements that are largely inherited from single-sector models. Drawing on recent One Health governance scholarship, World Health Organization policy, and WIPO institutional IP policy guidance, this article proposes a One Health IP architecture built on cross-sector ownership rules, field-sensitive licensing, access and stewardship clauses, interoperable data governance, environmental performance obligations, and accountability-linked financing. The argument is policy-advocacy oriented: One Health will remain normatively compelling but operationally weak unless public institutions redesign the legal and translational infrastructure that governs invention, diffusion, and public-interest commercialization.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the information content of the time required to fund a fintech loan on credit allocation, listing quality, and platform screening outcomes. Using granular loan-level data from Prosper Marketplace, we show that funding time reflects how credit is allocated across different combinations of borrower risk and loan return, and that this relationship is highly dependent on monetary policy regimes. During the Pre-COVID and the subsequent monetary easing periods, higher-risk, higher-return listings were funded more quickly, suggesting that investor risk appetite for such loans was high. Whereas during the later period of monetary tightening, those loans took considerably longer to fund, as investors were more cautious and focused on higher-quality borrowers. Moreover, we find that shorter funding time is associated with a lower likelihood of post-listing platform rejection during the Pre-COVID period, but this relationship weakens during monetary easing and reverses during monetary tightening. Finally, we do not find significant predictive power of funding time for loan delinquency. This suggests that Prosper fully incorporates the information contained in funding time when making the final post-listing loan screening.

detail.title: Hump-Shaped Incentives under Non-stationary Learning
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes optimal dynamic contracting when a firm's profitability follows an unobservable Markov chain and learning is non-stationary. Unlike standard models with constant learning rates, the principal's learning speed here varies endogenously with her belief, creating a novel trade-off between incentive provision and belief manipulation. We uncover the "peak-uncertainty principle": the optimal incentive intensity is hump-shaped in the principal's posterior belief. When beliefs are extreme, the manager lacks the "hiding space" to disguise shirking as bad luck; when uncertainty peaks at intermediate beliefs, the manager can most effectively manipulate the principal's learning process, necessitating a higher information rent premium. Furthermore, we show that state persistence is a key determinant of agency costs; higher persistence prolongs the manager's informational advantage. The optimal contract can be implemented via a dynamic capital structure featuring belief-dependent inside equity and revolving credit lines. Our results provide a theoretical foundation for the empirical patterns of CEO pay, "pay-for-luck," and turnover in industries with varying information opacity.

detail.abstract:
Clinical deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally constrained by their propensity to hallucinate—generating fluent but clinically unfounded assertions that pose direct patient safety risks. This work introduces Conditional Latent Routing (CLR), a compound inference architecture that decomposes clinical uncertainty into its aleatoric and epistemic constituents and applies distinct, mechanistically motivated interventions at each stratum. Inspired by the corollary discharge framework from computational psychiatry—wherein the healthy brain’s forward model suppresses self-generated sensory predictions, a mechanism whose dysfunction in schizophrenia produces hallucinations—we construct an analogous dual-pathway system for medical LLM inference. A fine-tuned Bio_ClinicalBERT encoder classifies input noise (aleatoric uncertainty) and routes clean inputs through a latent soft-prompting Fast Lane while directing noisy, contradictory records through a cautionary Slow Lane with explicit abstention instructions. To address epistemic uncertainty—the model’s internal confusion—we introduce a T-Adaptive Attention patch at the logits level that modulates generation temperature as an inverse function of hidden-state variance.

We evaluate CLR on BioMistral-7B across 400 clinical cases (200 clean, 200 noisy) using RAGAS Faithfulness scored by Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct via Groq API. Phase 1 (Aleatoric Routing) achieves 100% routing accuracy and 64.8% faithfulness on clean data with zero alignment tax, but reveals a critical failure: a 0% inconclusive rate on noisy inputs, indicating extreme over-helpfulness bias. Phase 2 (Epistemic T-Adaptive Patch) preserves faithfulness at 64.4% while demonstrating zero computational overhead, but the inconclusive rate remains at 0%. We formally prove this failure as The Greedy Paradox: under greedy decoding, temperature scaling of logits is mathematically nullified because  for all . Phase 3 (Non-Greedy Sampling) degrades faithfulness to 58.5% while still failing to trigger abstention, confirming that over-helpfulness bias is embedded in pre-training weight distributions, not merely in the decoding surface.

These results establish that single-agent, test-time interventions are fundamentally insufficient for self-uncertainty modulation in medical LLMs, providing strong empirical justification for transitioning to multi-agent systems with externalized uncertainty arbitration.

detail.title: Temporal Stability of the Bem Sex Role Inventory (BSRI)
detail.abstract: The Bem Sex Role Inventory (BSRI) is among the most widely used measures of gender identity in economic research, yet its original classification has not been tested in over two decades. We provide a contemporary validation of the BSRI's item classifications using Bem's original between-subjects elicitation procedure on an online U.S. adult sample. Of the 40 gendered items, 38 retain their original classification: all 20 masculine items are confirmed, and 18 of 20 feminine items remain feminine. No item reverses direction. Yet the magnitude of desirability gaps has gradually attenuated since the original study, with female raters driving much of this compression. Our findings indicate that while the directions of the BSRI remain intact, the intensity of gender differentiation has weakened over time.

detail.abstract: The Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) function is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies. Historically positioned as a backward-looking, data-processing unit, FP&A is increasingly expected to serve as a forward-looking strategic partner to senior leadership. This paper examines how AI is catalyzing this transition, exploring key dimensions including automation of routine tasks, enhancement of forecasting capabilities, evolution of the analyst's role, and organizational implications. Drawing on recent industry surveys, practitioner insights, and emerging literature, the paper argues that while AI adoption in FP&A is accelerating, the true transformation lies not in the technology itself but in the reimagination of the FP&A function as a center of strategic intelligence.

detail.abstract: This Article argues that modern wellness influencer marketing represents a digital revival of the American medicine show. From 19th-century patent medicine peddlers to today's social media personalities hawking detox teas and gummy supplements, wellness fraud has exploited the same information asymmetries, regulatory gaps, and cultural anxieties-while leveraging new technologies that amplify both reach and harm. The Article traces this evolution across five Parts: the history of American wellness fraud and current regulatory frameworks; the rise of modern wellness influencers and "conspirituality"; COVID-19 pandemic health scams; the institutional capture of government health agencies by wellness industry interests; and a critique of existing regulatory approaches with recommendations for reform. These recommendations include reforming the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, enhanced platform transparency requirements modeled on the European Union Digital Services Act, strengthened Federal Trade Commission enforcement authority, and targeted amendments to Section 230 that would remove immunity for algorithmically promoted health misinformation. The story of American wellness regulation is not one of scientific progress triumphing over quackery, but of a complex dance between innovation, exploitation, and institutional adaptation. Understanding this history is essential to developing regulatory frameworks capable of addressing contemporary wellness fraud while respecting legitimate interests in health autonomy and free expression.

detail.title: Discrimination Against Transgender Patients in Primary Care: Evidence from an Audit Study
detail.abstract: This paper tests for discrimination against transgender individuals seeking a new primary care appointment. We conduct an audit study of nearly 1,000 U.S. primary care providers by sending appointment requests that signal either transgender or cisgender identity through the relationship between the patient's legal and chosen names. We find no evidence of discrimination in overall response rates - transgender patients are actually slightly more likely to receive a response than cisgender patients - but significant discrimination in terms of the nature of the responses. Conditional on receiving a response, trans patients are 17 percentage points less likely to receive a positive response than cisgender patients. Trans patients are not significantly more likely to be outright rejected for an appointment, but have much higher rates of ambiguous responses, where providers neither clearly offer nor deny an appointment but ask for more information or direct individuals to complete additional forms.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the productivity in Danish primary and lower secondary schools, comparing both private and public schools for the school year 2023/2024. The analysis is conducted at a school level using the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) method. In the main model (model 1), the input variables are salary expenses and a socioeconomic reference (expected grade point average on school-level based on pupils’ individual socioeconomic background), where the purpose of the socioeconomic reference is to ensure comparability between schools. The output variables are the actual grade point average, the share of pupils receiving special education in a normal classroom and the share of pupils receiving special education in a separate special class. The main model shows an average input-oriented score of 0.72, meaning that salary costs could be reduced by 28% if all schools matched the productivity of the most efficient peers. The average output-oriented score was 1.11, which translates into that pupil performance could increase by 0.8 grade points (on a scale from -3 to +12). Additionally, private schools demonstrate significantly higher productivity than public schools. A second-stage Tobit regression model identifies key factors influencing productivity, revealing that school size, employee composition and pupil well-being/parent satisfaction are significantly correlated with school productivity.

detail.title: Second Opinions and the Return Option: Disclosure and Commitment in Credence Goods Markets
detail.abstract: We study second opinions in credence goods markets when consumers can disclose a prior recommendation. Standard models impose a no-going-back rule, implying that second opinions are sought in secrecy. Yet, in practice, especially in health care, prior visits are often disclosed. First, we develop a model in which, after receiving a second opinion, the consumer returns to the initial expert with an exogenously given probability. We show that when this probability exceeds a threshold, disclosure is incentive compatible, as it induces truthful recommendations by the second expert, which in turn alters the first expert's incentives in a non-trivial way. We then make the return probability endogenous in a doctor-patient setting, introducing a strategic commitment problem through the choice of distance, and show that if the cost of returning to the first doctor is not too high, the patient chooses a sufficiently distant second doctor, incurring travel costs that act as a commitment device to sustain a positive probability of return, making both disclosure and return incentive compatible in equilibrium.

title: Inflation, Central Bank Reaction, and Equity Trading Volumes: Closing the Missing Link Through Knightian Uncertainty in Monetary Policy

detail.title: Inflation, Central Bank Reaction, and Equity Trading Volumes: Closing the Missing Link Through Knightian Uncertainty in Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified theoretical framework connecting goods-market inflation to equity trading volumes through the central bank reaction function. The literature has long established two separate facts: trading volume and return volatility co-move with information arrival, generating leptokurtosis in asset returns (Clark, 1973; Epps and Epps, 1976; Tauchen and Pitts, 1983; Karpoff, 1987); and Knightian uncertainty-the absence of assignable probabilities-induces investor paralysis and collapses trading volume (Dow and Werlang, 1992). The theoretical bridge between goods-market inflation and these market-microstructure outcomes has, however, remained largely unspecified. We argue that this bridge runs through monetary policy: elevated or volatile inflation destabilises the central bank's reaction function, generating ambiguity-rather than mere quantifiable risk-over the future path of interest rates. Drawing on the event-study methodology of Bernanke and Kuttner (2005), which shows that unexpected Federal Reserve policy changes exert a quantitatively significant effect on equity prices and excess return expectations, we contend that it is the unpredictability of policy under high inflation that constitutes the Knightian dimension of monetary uncertainty. We formalise this chain through three layers: parameter uncertainty about the Taylor-rule coefficients, model uncertainty about the inflation regime, and preference uncertainty about the central bank's mandate trade-off. Each layer widens the set of priors held by rational investors in the sense of Dow and Werlang (1992), ultimately suppressing trading activity. The paper closes with an empirical strategy exploiting CPI announcement windows during the 2021-2023 Federal Reserve hiking cycle as a natural experiment.

detail.abstract: We analyse the portfolio-reallocation incentives faced by NIIP-surplus economies under cross-border seizure risk. Assets, such as gold, can be physically imported and held domestically in contrast to financial claims on other jurisdictions. Gold purchases not only reduce the NIIP but can also drive steep increases in gold prices. We review the history of gold as an international settlement asset, the evolution of financial sanctions, and the global distribution of NIIP and gold holdings. We calibrate a simple model to recent gold mining cost curves and show that (assuming a current account balance of zero) closing one trillion dollars of NIIP per year through newly mined gold could push prices above USD 8,500 per ounce, while a ten-trillion-dollar target could be consistent with USD 67,000 per ounce. In an extended model, NIIP surplus countries face a trade-off between rapid NIIP reduction, with subsequent valuation losses, versus gradual adjustment, which tempers price impacts but lengthens the period of exposure to cross-border seizure risks. We also model the case of an elastic supply from mobilization of existing private holdings in the rest of the world via a simple portfolio reallocation channel.

title: Decolonizing the Frontline: Why INGOs Fail in Multi-Polar Warfare and Why Localization Is the Only Path to Survival

detail.abstract:
The classical INGO operational model — centralized command, international staff visibility, and neutrality declarations as access mechanisms — was designed for a world of unified sovereign authority. It is structurally incompatible with the multi-polar conflict environments that now define the majority of active humanitarian crises.

This paper introduces the Intermediary Paralysis Factor (Ωip), an original quantitative instrument that measures the rate at which centralized INGO networks fail under multi-actor disruption. The formula captures four variables: the number of distinct armed actors with veto power (N_actors), the mean hostility coefficient across actors (β_hostility), local operational capacity as the resilience denominator (C_local), the network redundancy score (γ_redundancy), and the population dependency coefficient (δ_dependency). When Ωip exceeds the critical threshold of 2.0, centralized INGO architecture is structurally unable to maintain operational access.

Three empirical theaters validate the framework. Yemen (2024–2026) produces Ωip > 3.8: 69+ UN staff arbitrarily detained, one WFP worker killed in detention, operations suspended across governorates, and 80% of the population losing access to aid alternatives. The Afghanistan-Iran forced displacement corridor (2024–2026) produces Ωip ~ 2.4: 2.8 million Afghans deported from Iran with zero INGO access to processing centers and local absorption capacity at zero. Sudan (2023–2025) produces Ωip ~ 3.2: RSF-SAF dual control environment, systematic aid diversion and taxation, and 7.4 million internally displaced with collapsing humanitarian space.

The paper proposes the Distributed Resilience Architecture as the structural remedy: a localized, redundant operational model in which γ_redundancy — the network's capacity to absorb INGO exit without service collapse — becomes the primary organizational performance metric. Localization is not an ideological preference. In multi-polar conflict environments, it is the only operational architecture capable of surviving the conditions that define contemporary humanitarian frontlines.

detail.abstract:
Throughout history, Black communities in the United States have faced aggressive and heightened policing, criminalization, and incarceration compared with their peers. At the same time, Black communities have been denied equal access to safe and affordable housing. Together, the criminal legal system and the housing sector create a reinforcing feedback loop that traps people in a cycle of criminalization and homelessness. Due to historic and ongoing structural racism, Black people are disproportionately ensnared in this cycle, with serious consequences for community safety, public health, and civil rights. The Legal Defense Fund’s Thurgood Marshall Institute (TMI) envisions a future where government leaders address homelessness through the provision of housing and supportive services instead of punishment, and all people—regardless of their prior involvement with the criminal legal system—have access to safe communities and housing.

This Report offers two major contributions to existing literature on this subject. First, it centers the experiences of Black people within the criminalization and homelessness conversation, and grounds this conversation in the long history of anti-Black laws used to police the movement of Black people in public spaces. Second, it examines Atlanta, Georgia, as a case study in which the cycle of criminalization and homelessness plays out with devastating consequences for Black people, presenting original data analysis on racial disparities in arrests for vagrancy charges using nationwide and Atlanta-specific arrest data reported by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

detail.abstract:
This paper examines a structural challenge in Luxembourg’s macroprudential framework: the limited integration of housing-market risk monitoring, supervisory visibility, and emerging wholesale settlement innovation. As a highly interconnected AAA-rated financial centre, Luxembourg benefits from strong institutional foundations but faces growing pressures from housing affordability constraints, demographic change, cross-border labour dependence, and evolving financial-market infrastructure requirements.

The paper proposes a Supervisory Visibility Infrastructure (SVI) framework designed to strengthen macroprudential resilience through enhanced monitoring, data integration, and coordinated supervisory oversight. It argues that improving visibility across housing-market indicators, financial-sector exposures, and systemic risk channels can support earlier policy intervention and more effective risk management. The framework also explores the potential role of controlled wholesale settlement innovation within existing Eurosystem arrangements, emphasizing that central bank money remains the anchor of settlement and that any innovation should operate within established regulatory and monetary-policy boundaries.

In addition, the paper assesses institutional coordination among Luxembourg’s supervisory and macroprudential authorities, including the Comité du Risque Systémique (CdRS), and identifies opportunities to improve information-sharing, escalation pathways, and operational preparedness. Rather than advocating radical structural change, the paper presents a phased and pragmatic policy blueprint aimed at strengthening resilience, preserving financial stability, and supporting Luxembourg’s long-term competitiveness as an international financial centre.

detail.abstract: This working paper  seeks to design an empirical strategy to assess the causal effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on gender gaps in employment and unemployment in OECD countries. To this end, a difference-indifferences design is proposed with panel data for 38 OECD countries during 2015-2021, comparing 2015-2019 (pre-COVID) with 2020-2021 (post-COVID). Control variables include human capital, total factor productivity, population, and GDP per capita. Preliminary results suggest a heterogeneous pattern rather than a systematic widening of gender gaps. Statistically significant reductions are observed for the total unemployment gap, the youth unemployment gap (15-24 years), and the adult employment gap (15-64 years). In contrast, a statistically significant increase is observed for the youth employment gap (15-24 years). The total employment gap and adult unemployment gap show no statistically significant effects. Preliminary conclusion: The pandemic did not uniformly widen gender gaps. Instead, it generated a heterogeneous pattern of convergence and divergence depending on the age group and labor indicator considered. Recovery policies with a gender perspective should consider age-specific interventions. These findings require confirmation with extended data and additional robustness analysis.

detail.abstract: The internal rate of return (IRR) is a ubiquitous performance statistic and decision making criterion in corporate finance and private markets. We provide four results that formalize, sharpen, and expand long-standing critiques of the IRR. We show that in a perfectly competitive market where there is an infinite supply of capital for positive NPV projects, the IRR decision rule will fail for every project. Moreover, we demonstrate that the previously identified pathologies of the IRR decision rule will emerge for any positive NPV project as long as financing is allowed. Taken together, our results imply that the IRR should not be used or taught as an (auxiliary) decision making criterion nor as a performance statistic. It should be used as a sensitivity analysis tool only.

detail.title: Noise-Suppressed Contrastive Learning for Cross-Language Code Clone Detection
detail.abstract: In real-world engineering software, source code is often cluttered with extensive noise data irrelevant to the core logic, such as comments, debugging statements, redundant code fragments, template codes, and logging outputs. This noise severely interferes with cross-language code clone detection models that rely on syntactic or semantic similarity, causing the high accuracy demonstrated by most existing methods on idealized datasets to degrade significantly in practical scenarios, while also presenting severe challenges to their generalization capability and robustness. To address these challenges, we propose NSCLC, an adaptive noise-suppression framework with two key components:CEN(CodeEnhanceNet) and a triplet-based contrastive learning mechanism. CEN employs multi-head cross-layer attention to model deep contextual dependencies within code, featuring an adaptive noise-suppression and semantic enhancement architecture that autonomously identifies and prunes non-functional tokens while reinforcing cross-lingual semantic consistency. The triplet-based contrastive learning mechanism then optimizes the latent representation space, enabling robust resilience against diverse types and intensities of interference. Experimental results on the AtCoder dataset show that our method achieves a Precision of 0.98, a Recall of 0.99, and an F1-score of 0.99, reaching a new state-of-the-art. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the CEN architecture, demonstrating robust stability and generalization across noise-intensive scenarios, including variable renaming, log statement insertion, statement swapping, and redundant statement deletion.

title: When Uncertainty Raises Hiring

detail.title: When Uncertainty Raises Hiring
detail.abstract: We study when productivity volatility raises hiring. In the U.S., total productivity volatility predicts higher unemployment and lower labor-market tightness. After removing the component explained by current aggregate conditions and their recent history, however, volatility predicts lower unemployment, higher tightness, and higher job finding. We develop a labor search model with aggregate productivity risk, match-specific productivity, hiring costs, and flexible or sticky wage setting. Volatility affects job finding through state-dependent hiring cutoffs and vacancy creation. The aggregate response is positive when these margins improve in states with large unemployment weight. Sticky wages amplify this response by limiting pass-through of surplus gains to workers.

שקיפות בעידן הבינה המלאכותית: המשפט הישראלי
Transparency in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: The Israeli Legal Perspective
detail.abstract:
In recent years, there has been significant growth in the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Despite its efficiency, AI usage presents challenges, particularly in places where decisions have significant implications for human rights. This article focuses on algorithmic transparency in the AI era in the context of the right to freedom of information of government authorities.

Within this framework, the article examines the principles of transparency concerning the right to information in the AI era. It examines how Israeli courts address this issue regarding traditional algorithms, and how it affects the AI era. The article advocates recognizing algorithmic transparency as part of the right to freedom of information, considering both the language and the purpose of the law, and considering global trends advocating transparency in artificial intelligence. Algorithmic transparency as part of the right to freedom of information is crucial to enable continued effective oversight of government authorities’ actions.

title: Beyond Objective Measures: Subjective Wellbeing and Life Satisfaction among Youth

detail.title: Beyond Objective Measures: Subjective Wellbeing and Life Satisfaction among Youth
detail.abstract: The study aims to address the gap between measures of individual wellbeing using Subjective Wellbeing (SWB), moving beyond the traditional measures to understand the extent to which material conditions contribute to perceived life satisfaction. Drawing from the primary data collected from the age group 18-29, this study uses the India Youth Development Index (YDI) and Personal wellbeing Index (PWI). The findings of the study reveal the incongruity between the objective and subjective wellbeing measure. Where objective measures suggest the moderate but uneven wellbeing among the participants, subjective wellbeing is reported consistently high. The mismatch between OWB and SWB is more visible in domain-level analysis, especially between low objective wellbeing in community participation, social justice and employment domains, parallel to consistent high subjective wellbeing, in relationship, community and achieving domains. Qualitative findings suggest the role of relationships and social support, central to subjective wellbeing. The study contributes to the larger wellbeing domain by highlighting the domainspecific and youth-focused evidence and advocating the need to bridge subjective and objective measures in assessing human development.

detail.abstract: Malaria remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Nigeria, particularly among children under five, despite ongoing control efforts. The introduction of malaria vaccines (RTS, S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M) offers a new preventive strategy. This systematic review assessed the status of malaria vaccine rollout in Nigeria, focusing on implementation, awareness, acceptance, and health system readiness. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and grey literature (2015–2026) identified 12 eligible studies involving caregivers, healthcare workers, and national programme data. Vaccine acceptance among caregivers was consistently high, ranging from 76.6% to 95.6%, with generally positive perceptions across regions. However, awareness levels were highly variable, ranging from 9.7% in Lagos to 79.6% among hospital pharmacists. Vaccine-specific awareness, such as recognition of R21/Matrix-M, was low (15.5% in some populations). Among healthcare workers, physicians demonstrated 68.9% adequate knowledge, whereas nurses showed predominantly poor knowledge. Pharmacists reported 79.6% awareness but expressed concerns regarding vaccine safety and efficacy. Health system readiness remained limited, with facility preparedness scores in northern Nigeria ranging from 33% to 51%. Nigeria demonstrates strong malaria vaccines acceptance but persistent gaps in awareness, knowledge, and implementation capacity. Strengthening health systems and addressing operational constraints are essential for successful malaria vaccine rollout.

detail.title: Heterogeneous Interest Rate Sensitivity across Industries and States
detail.abstract: This paper examines employment responses to monetary policy across U.S. industries and states using quarterly state–industry panel data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) spanning 1990–2023. Using local projection instrumental variable (LP-IV) methods with high-frequency monetary policy surprises as instruments for federal funds rate changes, I find substantial heterogeneity in cumulative employment responses across sectors and regions. While monetary tightening reduces aggregate employment, the average response masks large differences across sectors and regions. Administrative services, construction, and durable goods manufacturing exhibit the largest cumulative employment declines following monetary tightening, while utilities, arts and entertainment, and health care display comparatively small responses. States also differ markedly in their employment responses to monetary policy.

detail.title: Sex Differences in Socioeconomic Inequalities in Diabetes Prevalence Across 30 European Countries: A Sex-Stratified Multi-Dimensional Analysis of the WHO Health Inequality Data Repository

detail.abstract:
Background: Diabetes disproportionately burdens socioeconomically disadvantaged populations, yet whether this inequality differs by sex across Europe remains poorly characterised. We quantified sex-stratified diabetes inequality across 30 European countries. 

Methods: We analysed WHO Health Inequality Data Repository (HIDR) Eurostat data (2014 and 2019; n = 30 countries). Absolute inequality was measured using the concentration index D. Sex differences were tested with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and quantified using Hodges-Lehmann estimators. Cross-dimensional consistency was assessed with Spearman rank correlations. Ecological regression examined GDP, Gini coefficient, female employment, and obesity prevalence as predictors. 

Findings: In 2019, female D exceeded male D in 20 of 30 countries for economic inequality (median: 7·4 pp [IQR 5·5–9·3] vs 5·4 pp [IQR 3·8–7·1]; Hodges-Lehmann 1·70 pp; rank-biserial r = 0·557 [large]; p = 0·007) and in 28 of 30 countries for education (Hodges-Lehmann 2·80 pp; r = 0·897; p < 0·001). No significant sex difference was observed for place of residence (p = 0·608). Cross-dimensional consistency was confirmed by positive Spearman correlations between economic, education, and age dimensions (r = 0·51–0·52; BH-adjusted p < 0·05). Eastern European countries had the highest female economic D (median 10·2 pp). GDP per capita was the only significant ecological predictor (WLS R² = 35·2%; β = −2·35 per log-unit, p < 0·001). 

Interpretation: Women in lower socioeconomic positions bear a disproportionate diabetes burden across Europe, concentrated in Eastern Europe. Sex differences are consistent across economic and education dimensions. Gender-sensitive interventions are needed.

title: Bound by Tradition: Cultural Gender Norms and Occupational Choice
affiliations: Lund University

detail.title: Bound by Tradition: Cultural Gender Norms and Occupational Choice
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether cultural gender norms about occupations, defined as a society's perception of what is appropriate work for men and women, contribute to persistent gender-stereotypical occupational choice. Using large-scale international survey data and high-quality administrative records, I study whether second-generation immigrant men (women) are less likely to work in an occupation that is perceived as female (male)-typical work in their country of ancestry. I find robust evidence that men, but not women, adhere to occupation-specific cultural gender norms: men are less likely to work in an occupation that is perceived as female work in their country of ancestry, while there is no such effect for women. To investigate mechanisms behind this result, I design an international survey experiment. The results corroborate the gender asymmetry found in the observational data and reveal a social perception penalty for men in heavily female-dominated occupations, but no comparable consistent penalty for women in male-dominated fields. Taken together, the findings of this paper suggest that persistent social norms are a key factor behind the slow integration of men into female-dominated occupations.

detail.abstract: In today's digital landscape, social media marketing has become a powerful tool for businesses to engage customers and drive sales. This study marks the first empirical investigation in Albania on the influence of social media marketing on e-commerce sales and e-loyalty. The primary objective of this research is to examine the relationship between social media marketing, e-commerce sales, and e-loyalty within the Albanian context. The marketing in various social media platforms, such as Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, are examined to determine their effects on e-commerce sales and e-loyalty. The study employs a quantitative approach, utilizing a sample of 183 subjects, representing a diverse cross-section of the Albanian e-commerce sector. Data were analyzed using factor analysis, correlation and regression models. The results of the study demonstrated a significant positive impact of social media marketing on both e-commerce sales and e-loyalty. The findings revealed that businesses that effectively utilize social media marketing strategies experience higher levels of e-commerce sales and foster greater customer loyalty compared to those with limited or ineffective social media presence. These outcomes offer valuable empirical insights and practical implications for businesses to develop effective strategies, enhance ecommerce performance, and foster long-term customer loyalty.

title: Ticket Scalping in the Digital Age: An Analysis of Regulatory Frameworks in India and the European Union

detail.title: Ticket Scalping in the Digital Age: An Analysis of Regulatory Frameworks in India and the European Union
detail.abstract: The phenomenon of ticket scalping, where tickets for concerts, sporting events, and other live performances are resold at exorbitant prices by intermediaries, has emerged as a significant challenge for consumer protection in the digital era. In India, the absence of a robust regulatory framework leaves consumers vulnerable to exploitative practices, as recent controversies surrounding high-profile concerts such as Coldplay and Diljit Dosanjh have demonstrated. By contrast, the European Union has undertaken regulatory measures, including consumer protection directives and specific restrictions on automated ticket-buying software (“bots”), to address the distortions caused by scalpers in the entertainment market. This paper undertakes a comparative analysis of Indian and EU consumer law frameworks, examining how each jurisdiction conceptualises the consumer in the context of secondary ticket markets, and the extent to which existing laws address issues of unfair trade practices, contractual imbalance, and access to cultural goods. Drawing upon statutory provisions, judicial decisions, and policy interventions, the study argues that while the EU offers more developed protections against scalping, both systems reveal gaps in balancing market efficiency with consumer fairness. The paper also engages with broader normative questions that whether cultural participation should be treated as a consumer right, the role of digital platforms in regulating resale markets, and the ethical dimensions of profiteering from scarcity. In conclusion, the paper proposes a model framework for India inspired by EU practices, advocating for legislative clarity, stronger enforcement, and a consumer-centric approach to ensure fair access to entertainment and cultural experiences.

publicationDetails.detailsText: University at Buffalo School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-028

detail.abstract:
In his book Poverty Law and Legal Activism, Adam Gearey studies a prime period of 20 th century U.S. poverty law to illuminate critical legal studies as a theory of activism. Gearey recounts how radical anti-poverty lawyers of the 1960s and 1970s reflected on their work with clients as a process of seeing and struggling together with "lives that slide out of view." This essay explores how today's critical legal activists and academics continue this commitment to developing law's transformative power. 

Turning from academia to poverty lawyering as a ground for legal theory, Gearey offers a refreshing response to the idea that critique is an "an unaffordable luxury." Critical Legal Studies has been faulted for taking a "traditionally elitist approach to law by remaining confined within elite institutions and purveyed by law professors, sometimes in impenetrable language." By focusing on the everyday struggles of poverty law work, Gearey identifies legal critique not only as thinking about law, but as a practice of changing what we do and who we are. 

This vision suggests how critique can respond to the current era's multiple crises in the face of a tidal wave of disdain for reason, law, and democracy. Across the political spectrum, a widespread culture of fear, division, and distraction seduces people into complicity with systems of personal and mass destruction. In this context, social change will require more than revealing the irrationality and injustice of existing institutions or defending noble moral principles. It will also require collective practices of learning and caring to generate power for good.

This essay begins by turning to contemporary social movements working to transform the structures keeping many lives and communities “in close proximity to death,” as Gearey describes the condition of poverty. Three themes from contemporary grassroots activism can guide legal responses to today’s human and environmental disasters. First, solutions to poverty require a comprehensive redesign of law, politics, and economy, not simply targeted inclusion or redistribution within existing institutions. Second, collective transformative praxis is fundamental to resisting poverty and other socioeconomic harms. Third, political economic transformation involves affirming and redirecting law’s structural power.

Next, this essay situates today’s struggles for socioeconomic justice in a context of disillusionment with legal liberalism’s capacity to correct the systemic failures underlying poverty. The law-and-economics school of thought answers liberal law’s shortcomings with a deceptive ideal of efficiency. That ideal has helped to rationalize and amplify conditions of growing inequality and insecurity, fueling popular support for authoritarianism. Critique must now challenge both the liberal ideal of law’s neutrality and the neoliberal and illiberal valorization of law’s inequality.

The final section considers how critical theory can follow activists’ lead in affirming law’s power for social and economic justice. I highlight two recent strands of critical theory, one focused on human vulnerability and the other on money, both of which offer ambitious visions for changing the systems that make poverty and other catastrophic conditions appear reasonable, tangential, or intractable.

detail.abstract: We document and explain the gap between measures of AI exposure and measures of AI adoption in the workplace. This leads us to propose a new AI adoption index based on comparative advantage. Using the representative German DiWaBe employee survey linked to worker and establishment information, we compare worker-reported AI use to prominent exposure measures and find that the relationship is weak. Motivated by this gap, we develop a framework in which adoption depends not only on technical feasibility-AI's absolute advantage measured by exposure-but on profitability-AI's comparative (dis)advantage relative to a specific worker-balancing AI productivity against AI user costs and worker productivity against wages. We operationalize this framework at the task level by (i) estimating worker productivity relative to pay, (ii) mapping exposure indices into AI productivity, and (iii) inferring task-specific AI user costs from revealed-preference adoption. The resulting occupation-level index accounts for 60% of cross-occupation variation in observed AI adoption, compared to 14% for an exposure-only model. The two approaches diverge substantially for approximately 30% of workers, highlighting that comparative advantage-not exposure alone-is crucial for assessing AI's labor-market impact. * We thank Christina Patterson for an insightful discussion. We benefited from comments by audiences at the Women in Macro Conference 2026 and the Montreal Workshop on Markets with Frictions 2026. The data access was provided via on-site use at the Research Data Centre (FDZ) of the German Federal Employment Agency (BA) at the Institute for Employment Research (IAB) and remote data execution.

detail.abstract: Private credit funds have emerged as major players in corporate lending and protection sales to banks within the SRT market. This paper models a contagion loop between the banking system and private credit funds working through SRTs. The loop is activated by two elements whose interaction is scarcely formalised in the literature: the circular leverage embedded in SRT financing and the liquidity mismatch introduced by semiliquid private credit funds. Together, they can result in shrinking protection for banks, i.e. a protection gap. Implemented through a simulation, the model provides evidence on the impact of this mechanism on banks' capital relief and lending capacity, and represents a useful risk-assessment tool to both private and public agents.

detail.abstract:
This article is a response to Professors Matthew Lawrence and David Pozen’s Drug Scheduling as Institutional Design, in a spirit of engagement rather than opposition. The goal of this response is not to contest their central framework. Rather, we seek to identify several context-dependent areas that bear on the ultimate success of the suggested reforms and the Article’s institutional account — especially for readers less familiar with the operational details at the intersection of drug law and health regulation. The Parts that follow elaborate these considerations.

Part I situates the Article’s institutional design framework within a broader interdisciplinary literature and examines the demands that a pragmatic institutional approach imposes, emphasizing the need for grounding in the operational complexity of contemporary drug regulation. Part II clarifies the distribution of authority among federal agencies and why those allocations matter for scheduling reform. Part III turns to practitioners and enforcement dynamics, exploring how prescribing regulation and criminal enforcement shape the institutional environment in which reform would operate. Part IV considers opioid treatment programs and harm reduction as institutional case studies, particularly regarding proposed Schedule A, and Part V assesses whether the Article’s proposed reforms constitute structural redesign or incremental layering within the CSA framework.

title: Informal Housing and Self-help Spatial Practices under Compound Risk in Lisbon’s Urban Periphery
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Informal Housing and Self-help Spatial Practices under Compound Risk in Lisbon’s Urban Periphery
detail.abstract: Informal and self-built housing in urban peripheries is increasingly exposed to compound risks produced by the interaction of climatic hazards, public-health crises, infrastructural deficits and socio-spatial vulnerability. This article examines Santa Marta de Corroios, a self-built neighbourhood in the municipality of Seixal, in Lisbon’s urban periphery, as an exploratory qualitative case study of informal housing under compound risk. The COVID-19 pandemic is treated not as an isolated crisis, but as a stress test that exposed the limits of public-health measures assuming the home could function as a safe space for isolation, hygiene, care, remote work and schooling. Based on field observation, photographic records, semi-structured conversations, a focus-group walk with women members of the residents’ association, and housing and demographic data provided by local actors, the article analyses how residents identify and respond to overlapping pandemic, climatic and housing-related vulnerabilities. The findings show that interventions in roofs, patios, thresholds, openings, drainage paths and domestic layouts are not framed locally as formal disaster risk reduction or planned climate adaptation. Nevertheless, they can be interpreted as self-help spatial practices: incremental, experience-based adjustments through which households and community members partially reduce exposure to flooding, overheating, poor ventilation, spatial overcrowding and storm-related damage. The article argues that these practices should not be romanticised as substitutes for public investment, but they provide situated knowledge for more effective, health-responsive and climate-adaptive upgrading strategies in precarious urban territories.
