detail.abstract:
As a drafter of Part 12, I examine the regulation on Commercial Acquisitions in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) from its origins to the changes proposed by the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO).  The article is divided into: issues writing Part 12, the maintenance of Part 12, and the RFO proposed changes. 

Issues drafting Part 12:  The section is limited to:
Individuals with expertise in Simplified Acquisition and individuals with expertise in Major Systems Acquisition drafted Part 12.  The Simplified Acquisition group focused on volume, while the Major Systems group focused on individual contracts for high-dollar purchases.  The Simplified Acquisition group created the SF 1449 for small-dollar buys; the Major System group agreed to require only the SF 1449. 

The definition of Commercial Items in the Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act (FASA):  This definition includes more than one type of product and commercial services.  Well-developed commercial marketplaces with multiple sellers adequately protect buyers.  However, buyer protections may be weakened when acquiring newly offered items or items with unique governmental modifications. So, Part 12 was written for commercial products that are most like Commercial-off-the-Shelf (COTS) items.  Also, Part 12 was not written for the acquisition of commercial services.     

Terms and conditions (T&Cs):   No standard set of T&Cs exists in the commercial marketplace.  The relative strength of buyers and sellers controls T&Cs.  Also, different commercial markets have different T&Cs.  FAR 52.212-4, Contract Terms and Conditions-Commercial Items, balances seller and buyer commercial T&Cs, concepts from FAR clauses, and principles from the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) to create a generic clause for commercial products.   Tailoring allows contracting officers to modify FAR 52.212-4 for a particular marketplace without deviations; waivers limit the addition of T&Cs inconsistent with the commercial marketplace practices.

Maintenance of Part 12:  The FAR Council limited the flexibility of Part 12  by adding tables to Part 12 that appear to constraint tailoring. The FAR Council also placed the explanation of the flexibilities of Subpart 13.5, Simplified Procedures for Certain Commercial Items, in a Federal Register Notice and not the FAR.  Subpart 13.5 is an “other competitive procedure” that qualifies as “full and open” competition. 

Revolutionary FAR Overhaul: The delight of discovering Subpart 13.5 caused the RFO to conflate selected procedures from Part 13 into Part 12 and then limit Part 13 to noncommercial acquisitions.  Instead, Part 12 should contain policies unique to Commercial acquisitions and allow contracting officers to use any available procedure in the FAR.  The procedures mandated by the Competition in Contracting Act (CICA), not the FAR, create the hated complexity of government competitions.

detail.abstract: A select group of great innovators have produced more than one major contribution. These exceptional individuals are known far beyond their own disciplines, and are routinely described as unique. Yet although their extraordinary accomplishments obviously make them outliers, the processes by which they arrive at their discoveries follow patterns that are shared by innovators more generally. This paper examines these patterns for six great serial innovators of the modern era: the experimental Henry Ford, who worked tirelessly by trial and error to make better cars more efficiently, and the conceptual Albert Einstein, Pablo Picasso, Walt Disney, Miles Davis, and Steve Jobs, who formulated surprising new ideas and products by connecting previously unrelated elements. These contrasting methods of discovery resulted in sharply contrasting life cycles of creativity, as Einstein, Picasso, Disney, Davis, and Jobs all made major contributions during their 20s, but Ford did not make his first great innovation until he was 45.

detail.abstract: This study is motivated by the lack of proper study on estimating unconditional, direct, and time-varying tails for Hedge funds (HFs). Using an autoregressive conditional Fréchet model, we first estimate the asymmetric timevarying right and left tails for four HFs' strategies during 2005-2025. The left tails' reactions to the market crises suggest poor market timing in HFs, with the 2008 crisis generating the greatest tail jump. We then employ a time-varying parameter vector autoregression to study the response of HFs' left tail and performance to shocks in VIX, repo rate, Amihud liquidity, and real economic expectations. We compare the left tail responses to macroeconomic shocks of September 2008, February 2020 and September 2022. The results point to persistent homogeneous exposure to market crises. We also find that the 2022 crisis has a longer-lasting impact on HFs' tails, compared to the 2008 or 2020 crisis, implying lower resilience in the HF industry. The liquidity shocks take the longest to dissipate, and positive repo shocks curb the left tails acting as a buffer against market crises. Since 2022, repo shocks trigger greater responses in HFs' performance. While Equity Hedge benefits from turbulent market, calm market drives up Event-driven performance.

title: The Daughters of Disaster: Famine, Gender Preferences, and Cohort Sex Ratios in China
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: The Daughters of Disaster: Famine, Gender Preferences, and Cohort Sex Ratios in China
detail.abstract: Disasters can reshape social preferences in ways that persist long after the immediate crisis has passed. This paper studies whether China's Great Famine, from 1959 to 1961, durably shifted family preferences toward daughters. Using prefecture-by-cohort sex ratios from the 1990 Census, I find that famine severity predicts lower sex ratios primarily among post-famine cohorts born from 1963 to 1970, not only among famine-born cohorts. This pattern is robust to alternative famine measures, province exclusions, and migration corrections. Fertility histories show that women from harder-hit areas reported fewer sons among both births and surviving children, with postnatal losses rising more for boys. A nationally representative social survey reveals that respondents in more affected areas express stronger daughter preferences, without a corresponding shift toward broader gender egalitarianism. These findings show that catastrophic shocks can reshape child-gender valuation, generating persistent daughter preference in China despite its long-standing son preference.

title: When Work Becomes Non-Viable: Cost-of-Participation Shocks and Systemic Labor Contraction

detail.title: When Work Becomes Non-Viable: Cost-of-Participation Shocks and Systemic Labor Contraction
detail.abstract:
Labor-market stability can mask a constraint when participation costs rise faster than returns to labor. This study introduces an SIR-macro framework to model Resource Lock, a threshold where work becomes financially non-viable for workers near subsistence margins. Using observed retail pricing across all 50 states in the United States, the framework links cost shocks to labor withdrawal, economic contraction, and permanent exit.

The system yields a combined Q3–Q4 2026 GDP decay of $257.4 billion, with $75.7 billion direct and $181.7 billion indirect, indicating that most contraction arises through downstream propagation. The model identifies 1.2 million permanent exits and a $105 billion productivity loss, concentrated in Tier I states.

These results suggest labor participation can shift discretely under cost pressure, producing nonlinear withdrawal, system-wide losses, and structural scarring while linking retail price dynamics to macroeconomic outcomes.

title: Impacts of Dobbs v. Jackson on Medical Residency Training

detail.title: Impacts of Dobbs v. Jackson on Medical Residency Training

detail.abstract: Using national data on outcomes of the National Resident Matching Program between 2019-2024 and a difference-in-differences approach, this study examines the effects of state abortion restrictions enabled by the US Supreme Court Decision in Dobbs v. Jackson on the supply of medical residents to training programs located in states restricting abortion. There was a significant decline in the supply of medical residents to abortion restricting states, primarily among those training in obstetrics and gynecology. Less able to fill quotas for new residents, residency programs entered subsequent Match cycles with smaller quotas and relied on comparatively less-competitive applicants to fill them. The share of female residents practicing in restrictive states also declined with the exception of more prestigious hospitals, which maintained similar cohort sex composition pre-post restriction. Findings carry both short and long-term implications for care access. Residents are a key provider for vulnerable populations, commonly staffing free and student-run clinics and taking on large shares of Medicaid and charity care patients in hospital settings, and, residency location is highly predictive of future practice patterns, so impacts on resident labor can drive long term consequences for future provider availability. Incentive programs such as loan repayment and location-specific subsidies may be useful tools in correcting reductions in the resident workforce across states where abortion is illegal.

detail.abstract:
Question: Did a physician quality metric and financial incentive for hypertension control improve clinical care and patient health? 

Findings: In this observational, difference-in-differences study, the financial incentive increased blood pressure re-measurement-an increase in guideline adherence-with no other impacts in the overall hypertensive population. Among patients with marginally high blood pressure, the financial incentive increased blood pressure re-measurement which improved documented rates of hypertension control, but also reduced medication adjustments and increased hospitalizations for acute cardiovascular events. 

Meaning: While the hypertension control financial incentive improved guideline adherent blood pressure measurement, it produced unintended harms for patients at the treatment margin.

detail.abstract: Border carbon adjustments (BCAs) are intended to limit carbon leakage while protecting domestic industry, but governments differ over whether border charges should price total embodied emissions or only emissions above an intensity benchmark. We study this design choice in a plant level general equilibrium model of the global steel industry with heterogeneous technologies and vertical supply chains. A rate-based BCA is equivalent to an emissions charge combined with an implicit output subsidy. It therefore weakens the carbon-price signal, encourages reshuffling of cleaner output toward the regulated market, and can induce leakage through underpriced carbon-intensive intermediates. In an EU-style setting with domestic carbon pricing, the rate-based design transmits only 36% of the mass-based border price needed to achieve the same global emissions reduction and yields larger welfare losses. In a US-style setting without a domestic carbon-price anchor, it mainly shifts rents toward domestic downstream industries rather than inducing abatement abroad.

title: Remedies in EU Competition Law: Between Caution, Creativity and Structural Change
affiliations: Tilburg Law and Economics Center (TILEC)

detail.title: Remedies in EU Competition Law: Between Caution, Creativity and Structural Change
detail.abstract: Remedies are central to EU competition law enforcement: without them, identifying anticompetitive conduct is largely futile. Yet the Commission's remedial record in digital markets-exemplified by Microsoft, Google Shopping, and Google Androidreveals a systematic failure of the principles-based, behavioural approach it has long preferred. This article examines the legal framework under Regulation 1/2003, reviews the Commission's enforcement record, considers reform proposals from the academic literature, and argues that the Google AdTech proceedings illustrate why structural intervention has become unavoidable. It concludes with legislative and procedural recommendations.

title: Buying Stability: Civil Service Quotas and Elite Co-optation in Imperial China
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management and Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: Buying Stability: Civil Service Quotas and Elite Co-optation in Imperial China
detail.abstract: How do autocratic states buy political stability from elites, and what are the long-run costs? This paper examines the social and political consequences of the 1427 regional quota reform in the Ming Civil Service Examination System. Using a prefecture-level difference-in-differences design, we show that quota expansion increased social mobility and exam access, but lowered admission quality. The additional quotas were disproportionately absorbed by historically strong prefectures and local elites, suggesting elite co-optation. Quota expansion reduced elite-led rebellions in the short run, while having little effect on peasant uprisings. Extending the analysis to the full Ming dynasty, we find a dynamic reversal pattern. Regions receiving larger quota increases experienced more peasant uprisings in the late Ming, and this pattern remains robust to alternative prefecture-level exposure measures. Place based quotas helped the Ming state buy elite stability, but this political bargain may have shifted the costs of maintaining order onto ordinary peasants and contributed to long run popular instability.

title: The Information Gap in Food Trade Corridors

detail.title: The Information Gap in Food Trade Corridors
detail.abstract: Food trade corridors move products across jurisdictions through a chain of documentation — phytosanitary certificates, export permits, trade manifests, customs declarations, import clearances. This paper examines the structural gap between what trade documentation carries and what buyers at the destination need to understand about the product. Trade documentation confirms regulatory admissibility for movement. It does not carry producer-level product information — origin detail, production practices, compositional attributes, quality context, or health-relevant characteristics. The paper argues that product-level information is generated at source but does not travel through trade corridors in portable, reusable form.

title: Envelopment by Multi-Product Firms in Digital Markets: A Case Study of Microsoft's 2026 Expansion of the Microsoft 365 E3 and E5 Bundles
affiliations: Tilburg Law and Economics Center (TILEC)

detail.title: Envelopment by Multi-Product Firms in Digital Markets: A Case Study of Microsoft's 2026 Expansion of the Microsoft 365 E3 and E5 Bundles
detail.abstract: This paper examines, as a case study for competition authorities and policymakers, the competitive risks raised by the conduct of multi-product dominant firms in the digital sector that progressively absorb adjacent functionalities into the bundles they already supply to enterprise customers. The strategy-sometimes described in the economic literature as envelopment-has been a recurrent feature of digital markets for more than two decades. The paper takes as its principal example the announcement, on 4 December 2025, that Microsoft will inject into its Microsoft 365 E3 and E5 enterprise productivity suites a substantial bundle of previously stand-alone, paid-for functionalities-including a remote-assistance product, advanced unified-endpoint-management features, endpoint privilege management, enterprise application management, public-key infrastructure, an email-security tier, and an AI-assisted security operations product-in exchange for an incremental price of three dollars per user per month, with effect from 1 July 2026. The paper sets out the economic mechanism by which conduct of this kind forecloses specialised singleproduct competitors, the empirical features of the market that make foreclosure particularly likely on the present facts, and the long-run consequences for competition and innovation. It identifies two analytical traps that competition authorities should expect dominant firms to exploit-the use of residual product lines to defeat coercion-based analysis, and the use of near-zero incremental cost in software markets to defeat cost-based screens.

detail.abstract: This chapter offers a comprehensive overview of central bank lender-of-last-resort law. It identifies eleven key elements of last-resort lending law, explains at a high level how these elements interact with one another and with other aspects of banking and finance law, and sketches the current global landscape. It then offers a history of last resort lending law, tracing its evolution around the world over the past several centuries. It concludes with a detailed case study of last resort lending law in the United States and the rise of the global dollar system, drawing on the U.S. experience to illustrate how legal design works in practice.

title: Geographic Indication Without Disclosure Depth

detail.title: Geographic Indication Without Disclosure Depth
detail.abstract: Geographic Indication (GI) systems protect the origin name of a product but do not structure the product-level information that makes the origin meaningful. This paper examines the structural gap between GI registration and the disclosure depth buyers, institutions, and consumers need to understand what distinguishes a GI product from a non-GI alternative. The paper documents how GI protects a name while leaving practices, terroir attributes, heritage context, compositional characteristics, and production evidence unstructured and non-portable. A GI tag confirms origin jurisdiction. It does not constitute product-level disclosure.

detail.abstract: Art and fashion have long shaped how we define ourselves, perceive others, and experience emotion. Through creative expression, individuals interpret meanings and form consumption habits that influence how they interact with the world. African fashion has gained international visibility, offering insight into cultural symbolism, identity, and innovation. African textiles, in particular, carry socio-cultural meaning, spirituality, and economic contributions that transcend centuries. This raises an important question in creativity, culture, and commerce: "How do people cognitively and emotionally respond to fabrics, and how can these responses inform marketing strategy?" Neuroscience reveals that specific aesthetic features, such as color, contrast, symmetry, pattern, and composition, activate neural pathways associated with emotion, reward, and the processing of visually pleasing stimuli (Yu & Shepard, 1998; Zeki, 1999). Much of this research, and its application in consumer neuroscience, is grounded in Western studies and commercial environments, yet little is known about how these processes operate within African art and fashion contexts. The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI), a creative youth revolution, an expanding e-commerce surge, and a renewed cultural consciousness are driving a collective African fashion renaissance. detail.abstract: The aim of this paper is to apply frameworks of public finance and political economy to the government employee pension system in India that has evolved beginning with the Old Pension Scheme (OPS) to the New Pension Scheme (NPS) and, currently, the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS). The entire policy discourse around pension benefits to government employees is centered around the tradeoff between fiscal prudence and populist political decisions, that are devoid of rational fiscal considerations. The core problem addresses the tension between providing adequate retirement security and maintaining fiscal sustainability, as states like Bihar and Assam spend over 50% of tax revenue on pensions. Using comparative policy analysis and fiscal impact analysis methodologies, the study examines the degree to which electoral pressures and organized employee interest groups drive fiscally unsustainable pension promises.

title: Pooling Together or Pulling Apart? The Effect of Mobile Money on Standard of Living Inequality in Kenya
affiliations: and SUNY New Paltz

detail.title: Pooling Together or Pulling Apart? The Effect of Mobile Money on Standard of Living Inequality in Kenya
detail.abstract: Over the past decades, mobile money (MM) has revolutionized access to financial services via mobile phones, especially for the financially excluded in developing countries. While existing research highlights MM's role in reducing income inequality at the crosscountry level, little is known about its impact on other dimensions of inequality at the subnational level. To close the research gap, this study investigates the effect of increased MM use on the inequality in standard of living in Kenya. Employing a methodological triangulation of quantitative analysis (System Generalized Method of Moments (System GMM)) and qualitative analysis (fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA)), this paper explores whether and how increased MM use interacts with socioeconomic factors to impact the inequality. The results of System GMM show that although increased MM use has no direct effect, the two-way interactions of MM and a range of socioeconomic factors are associated with the decreased inequality. The results of fsQCA further reveal that increased MM use narrows the inequality in socioeconomically developed regions, but not in less developed regions. Notably, this study documents a three-way configuration with strong explanatory power that increased MM use, in combination with high levels of economic development and traditional financial development, leads to the reduced inequality. These findings underscore the conjunctural and contingent nature of MM in equitable socioeconomic development and generate important policy implications.

title: Hyper-Personalisation in Retail Banking: Engagement, Retention and Commercial Growth
affiliations: , University College London and University College London

detail.title: Hyper-Personalisation in Retail Banking: Engagement, Retention and Commercial Growth
detail.abstract:
Hyper-personalisation leverages advanced analytics, AI, and real-time decisioning to deliver tailored products and interactions at the individual customer level. Fast-fashion brands have operationalised these capabilities through behaviour-led recommendations, adaptive experimentation, and personalised customer journeys, thereby driving loyalty, conversion, and profitability. Retail banks face similar pressures around retention, digital engagement, and competitive differentiation, but operate under stricter constraints around regulation, data privacy, suitability, explainability, financial well-being, and customer trust. As a result, they have been slower to adopt comparable behaviour-led engagement.
This paper examines how fast-fashion approaches to hyper-personalisation can be adapted for retail banking. It outlines emerging frameworks for converting behavioural data, predictive models, decision engines, and generative interfaces into personalised financial experiences, including predictive retention, intelligent advisory support, and iterative optimisation of customer engagement. 
Finally, the paper considers how these capabilities could transform retail banking from reactive service provision toward proactive, relationship-led financial ecosystems, with potential commercial impact through reduced attrition, deeper engagement, increased customer lifetime value, and improved operational efficiency.

title: Participation Elasticity and Economic Stability: A Multi-Channel Framework

detail.title: Participation Elasticity and Economic Stability: A Multi-Channel Framework

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract:
Economic growth no longer reliably translates into broad-based household income. This paper introduces participation elasticity (ε_p) as the single, policy-relevant parameter that quantifies how responsive participation income (P = W + R + T) is to changes in total output (Y):

ε_p = (ΔP / P) / (ΔY / Y) ≈ (ΔP / ΔY) × (Y / P)

where W = labor income, R = distributed capital income, and T = public transfer income.

When ε_p weakens below the calibrated stability threshold ε* ≈ 0.85, economies enter a self-reinforcing fragility loop: weak participation → insufficient demand → reliance on debt and asset inflation → amplified instability. Using proxy-based analysis, panel regressions (N=260, 2000–2025), and a Monte Carlo-calibrated Keynesian model (10,000 draws), we show the United States has fallen to ε_p ≈ 0.72 (well below ε*), while emerging markets (0.95–1.15), Nordic countries (0.95–1.10), refined Asian models (0.98 pooled), and Latin American models (0.97 pooled) remain robustly above the threshold.

Institutional moderators (union density, pension breadth, public capital ownership, state coordination) raise ε_p by 0.10–0.25 points. Open-economy policy simulations demonstrate that hybrid Nordic-Asian-Latin reforms lift ε_p by 0.20–0.35 points, reduce fragility risk from 31% to <3% under projected 2025–2030 slowdowns, and stabilize debt-to-GDP at modest fiscal cost (0.3–0.7% of GDP). Higher ε_p is also associated with substantially lower Gini coefficients of income inequality.

detail.abstract: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) ratings and sustainability-related data products have become increasingly important components of global financial markets, supporting investment decision-making, stewardship activities, sustainable finance, risk management, and corporate sustainability disclosures. As sustainability considerations become more deeply integrated into capital allocation decisions, regulators worldwide are increasingly focused on strengthening the transparency, governance, accountability, and integrity of ESG ratings markets while reducing the risk of greenwashing and information asymmetries. While this paper was initially developed in response to the Financial Sector Conduct Authority's (FSCA) Discussion Paper on ESG Rating Services and Data Providers in South Africa, it adopts a broader strategic perspective. The paper argues that ESG ratings should not be viewed merely as sustainability assessment tools, but as an emerging component of financial market infrastructure with important implications for capital mobilisation, sustainable finance, climate transition, market transparency, and long-term economic development. The analysis examines global regulatory developments across major jurisdictions, including the European Union, United Kingdom, India, Japan, Singapore, the United States, China and selected African markets. It explores the growing distinction between ESG ratings and traditional credit ratings, evaluates the role of ESG ratings in reducing information asymmetries and supporting capital formation, and considers the strategic importance of ESG ratings within the development of African sustainable finance ecosystems. The paper further argues that Africa has a unique opportunity to participate actively in the development of sustainability-related market infrastructure. Unlike the global credit ratings industry, which evolved largely without meaningful African participation, ESG ratings, sustainability data systems, green taxonomies, and sustainable finance frameworks remain at a formative stage of development. Consequently, policy decisions relating to ESG ratings regulation should be viewed not only through a compliance lens, but also through the broader objectives of strengthening market transparency, improving capital allocation, supporting climate transition, and enhancing Africa's participation within the evolving global sustainable finance architecture. Conclusions of this paper support the introduction of a formal, principles-based regulatory framework for ESG ratings and sustainability data providers that aligns with IOSCO recommendations and emerging international best practice. Such a framework should promote transparency, governance, accountability, and conflict-ofinterest management while preserving methodological diversity, analytical independence, innovation, and competition. The paper concludes that ESG ratings, sustainability disclosures, green taxonomies, and sustainability data systems are becoming increasingly interconnected pillars of sustainable finance architecture and that Africa has an opportunity to play a more active role in shaping their future development.

detail.abstract: We build new data on startups in Africa to study which types of financing these firms demand, how financing is allocated in practice, and the implications for startup creation and the composition of the sector. We combine a continent-wide founder survey, an incentive-compatible experiment estimating financing preferences, and venture capital (VC) deal records matched to founders' education and work histories. We find that startups strongly prefer equity over debt, but equity is supplied mainly by foreign investors and flows disproportionately to foreign-connected founders. About 80 percent of VC deals involve a foreign investor, and more than 60 percent of funded founders have studied or worked outside Africa. A simple accounting framework shows that this foreignness reflects three main forces: scarce local equity capital, a thin pool of local entrepreneurs able to access startup finance, and frictions limiting local entrepreneurs' access to foreign investors. Together, these forces reduce startup creation and tilt the sector toward foreign investors and foreign-connected founders.

detail.abstract: We introduce the AVC Theorem, proving that no system of autonomous AI supply chain agents can simultaneously satisfy Autonomy of optimization, signal Veracity, and decentralized Coordination. At most two of the three properties are simultaneously achievable. We show that AVC and the CAP Theorem in distributed computing are both instances of a General Impossibility Theorem for systems with private information and structural conflict (TGI), providing a formal unification rather than a merely conceptual analogy. We derive a critical sophistication threshold ν*, beyond which cooperative signaling becomes unsustainable, and establish that ν* is empirically calculable from observable market parameters. Recent evidence documents that frontier LLMs cross ν* in competitive environments within few interaction periods, making the theorem empirically relevant for currently deployed systems. We propose three falsifiable empirical predictions and introduce the Supply Chain Verification Protocol (SCVP), a cryptographic mechanism that partially restores coordination without sacrificing agent autonomy. For target journals Management Science and RAND Journal of Economics, we provide an illustrative difference-indifferences design exploiting M&A events in AI-intensive supply chains to identify Prediction P2.

detail.title: An Action-Valence Response Model for Operationalizing Peak-End Customer-Journey Design in Consumer E-Commerce
detail.abstract: Customer-journey measurement in modern consumer e-commerce predominantly aggregates satisfaction into a single journey-level score (NPS, CSAT) and treats individual journey interventions as candidates for isolated A/B testing. This stands in tension with a well-established finding from behavioral economics: customer memory of an experience is dominated by its emotional peak and by its end, not by averaged satisfaction across time [Kahneman et al., 1993, Fredrickson and Kahneman, 1993, Redelmeier et al., 2003]. We propose an operating methodology, the action-valence response model, that bridges this gap. The method instruments operating interventions in the customer journey at the action level, classifies each by its targeted journey position (peak, end, or baseline), measures emotional valence and cohort response to each deployed bundle, and fits a structural peak-end-weighted response surface. The methodology's central novelty-and the feature that makes it operationally executable rather than only conceptually sound-is the predictive model at the centre of the system: a regression on the empirical surface that produces forecasts of expected retention lift, with explicit standard errors, for every untested combination of peak and end interventions in the candidate space. Without this predictive capability, exhaustive testing of the candidate space would be infeasible: even a modest action library generates several hundred distinct bundles, and testing them sequentially against properly powered cohorts would consume years of operating time.

detail.title: Insider Trading in Prediction Markets: An Information-Participation Theory of Optimal Enforcement
detail.abstract: Prediction markets are valued for prices that aggregate dispersed information. Insider trading is distinctively corrosive: the trade that sharpens today's price drives out the crowd that makes tomorrow's price informative. We solve a microstructure model with a strategic insider and an endogenous, privately informed crowd facing a competitive market maker. Tougher enforcement curbs the insider, raising participation, so accuracy is hump-shaped and optimal enforcement is interior, neither laissez-faire nor a ban. The optimal intensity rises with the advantage's provenance: least for researched information, more for misappropriated information, and most for those who can move the outcome. Liquidity externalities can tip the market into a participation trap.

title: Value Contamination in Policy Simulation: Measuring How LLM Policy-Value Orientations Shape Predicted Administrative Burden Effects

detail.title: Value Contamination in Policy Simulation: Measuring How LLM Policy-Value Orientations Shape Predicted Administrative Burden Effects

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human subjects, human-subject recruitment, personally identifiable information, or private individual-level data. All individual profiles used in the simulations were synthetic and generated solely for experimental purposes. The empirical data consist of outputs produced by large language model APIs in response to standardized prompts. Because the study does not involve interaction with human participants or analysis of identifiable private information, formal institutional review board approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate behavioral responses to policy interventions, but their simulated treatment effects may depend on latent policy-value assumptions. This paper develops an audit framework for measuring value sensitivity in LLM-generated policy simulations. Using administrative burden in vaccination access as a testbed, I evaluate nine LLMs across six model families. Each model completes a policy-value orientation battery and then predicts vaccination willingness for 27 synthetic profiles under low-and high-burden access conditions. The results do not support a simple composite-contamination account. A composite policy-value contamination (PVC) index does not predict cross-model variation in administrative-burden effects. Dimension-specific checks suggest that collective obligation is positively associated with larger burden effects, contrary to the original PVC weighting, but this pattern is exploratory given the small number of model-level observations. Narrative frame-decomposition shows that access-barrier and coercive-backlash rationales are associated with larger burden effects, while collective-responsibility rationales are associated with smaller effects. The strongest evidence comes from a within-model frame-manipulation experiment: autonomy and equity/access frames increase predicted burden effects, whereas collective-obligation frames reduce them. The findings show that LLM policy simulations should not be treated as neutral behavioral forecasts, but neither are they well described by a single composite ideological score. Value sensitivity appears through specific orientation dimensions, expressed interpretive frames, and prompt-induced governance lenses. The paper contributes a framework for auditing LLM-based policy simulations by linking measured value orientations, simulated treatment effects, narrative mechanisms, and within-model frame responsiveness.

detail.title: Post-WWII U.S. Recessions and the 2026 Outlook: Examining the Economic Impact of a Proposed 25% Canada-Mexico Tariff
detail.abstract: Since World War II, the United States has experienced recurrent recessions driven by diverse shocks; energy price spikes, financial imbalances, policy tightening, and, most recently, the COVID-19 pandemic; with stabilization policy shaping their depth and duration. While the NBER dates recessions using a broad set of coincident indicators beyond the "two negative GDP quarters" rule, forward-looking financial variables often signal turning points earlier. In this paper, we assess how a potential 25% tariff on imports from Canada and Mexico could alter U.S. recession risk in 2026 within this postwar context. We make three contributions. First, we situate the current outlook in a historical perspective that links real activity, financial conditions, and policy responses. Second, we develop an empirically grounded forecasting framework that combines logistic regression with gradient boosting to estimate quarterly recession probabilities, leveraging both interpretability and nonlinear interactions. Third, we conduct scenario analysis that maps policyinduced shocks into six macroeconomic inputs; GDP growth, inflation, unemployment, consumer spending, trade balance, and the yield curve; using data from BEA, BLS, FHFA, FRED, the Conference Board, and the OECD. Our baseline scenario implies negligible recession risk throughout 2026. In contrast, a tariff scenario meaningfully raises risk, with probabilities rising from 12.5% in Q1 to 20.7% in Q4; under a combined scenario that layers additional adverse shocks, risk increases further to 18.3%-35.2%. These results underscore how trade policy can function as a macro shock, interacting with inflation dynamics, household incomes, and external demand; issues central to ongoing debates in economics and finance.

title: The Predictive Customer Equity Framework (PCEF): Integrating Machine Learning, Structural Econometrics, and Latent Affective State Variables for Enterprise Valuation in Retail

detail.title: The Predictive Customer Equity Framework (PCEF): Integrating Machine Learning, Structural Econometrics, and Latent Affective State Variables for Enterprise Valuation in Retail

keywords: Marketing Science Submission Classification: Original Research Article ~4

detail.abstract: Traditional methodologies for calculating Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) are predominantly retrospective and linear, treating retention as a stochastic process decoupled from internal organizational latency and the latent psychological states of the consumer. This paper introduces the Predictive Customer Equity Framework (PCEF), a multidisciplinary structural model that redefines customer portfolios as dynamic enterprise financial assets. By integrating deep learning architectures that continuously parse unstructured data streams with structural econometric discounting, we isolate a novel key variable: the Intrinsic Loyalty Coefficient (Λᵢ). This coefficient dynamically quantifies three latent affective state dimensions, specifically identity alignment, cognitive inertia, and satiation vulnerability, without direct or intrusive survey elicitation. The macro model further incorporates two internal firm constraints, the Data Hygiene Coefficient (αdata) and the Enterprise Transformation Index (βops), to capture operational drag. Through an empirical simulation study tracking 10,000 consumers over a 24-month horizon under competitive pricing shocks, we demonstrate that omitting internal operational modifiers and latent affective state vectors leads to structural mispricing of customer equity, frequently overvaluing opportunistic segments by more than 130 percent. Sensitivity analyses across seven parameterization scenarios confirm the directional robustness of this result. We provide mathematical optimization proofs confirming that maximizing Predictive Net Customer Equity (PNCE) yields superior long-term equilibrium net margins compared to traditional price-elasticity marketing models, offering a rigorous framework for strategic capital allocation.

detail.title: Recursive Intelligence: Human-AI Synergy and the Economics of Emergence A Working Paper

detail.abstract: The economics of artificial intelligence is built on a foundation that is not merely incomplete. It is wrong. And every cost-benefit analysis, organizational design decision, and governance framework constructed on top of it inherits that error in full. The two dominant frameworks, labor substitution and productivity augmentation, are organized around the wrong unit of analysis. Both treat AI as an input and humans as operators. Neither accounts for what actually happens when humans and AI systems engage in sustained iterative interaction: the emergence of intelligence, insight, and value that neither party could have produced independently, and that no conventional production function can model or measure. This paper advances two central claims. The first is that Human-AI Synergy, the recursive iterative co-production of human and artificial intelligence, constitutes a distinct economic category that existing frameworks cannot model or measure. The second is more provocative and more consequential: properly structured iterative human-AI collaboration does not merely make humans more productive. It makes them cognitively more capable, more creative, and more innovative. This is not a marginal efficiency gain. It is an expansion of the human cognitive frontier itself, a testable proposition that directly inverts the dominant cultural narrative and demands a new economic framework to analyze, measure, and govern. The failure to theorize recursive human-AI co-production is not a gap in the literature. It is a systematic misspecification with measurable consequences for how we design organizations, govern technology, and calculate what AI is actually worth.

detail.title: Enforcing Cooperation in Finitely Repeated Team Production: Theory and Experiments

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the Holmström's moral hazard in teams for environments where team production problems are repeated a finite number of times. Motivated by the observation that many real-world team interactions are naturally repeated while much of the literature emphasizes static peer-evaluation rules or repeated-game constructions that rely on infinite horizons, we adapt a Galbraith Mechanism (GM)-style allocation mechanism to a finitely repeated principal–agent team production setting and evaluate its performance both analytically and in the laboratory. We construct a repeated GM allocation that mixes equal sharing with proportional rewards, characterize subgame-perfect equilibria that sustain higher aggregate effort than static equal-share benchmarks, and design credible finite-horizon history-dependent punishments to select efficient equilibria when multiplicity arises. A laboratory experiment on a twice-repeated game tests the mechanism’s static and dynamic predictions under alternative allocation treatments. Our results show that groups under the (repeated GM) proportional allocation exert significantly higher effort than under (one-shot GM) equal sharing, consistent with theoretical predictions. Observed behavior indicates increased cooperation with repeated interaction.

detail.title: Place Effects in Health: Evidence from Rural-to-Urban Migrants in Sub-Saharan Africa
detail.abstract: This paper studies the health consequences of rural-to-urban migration, leveraging twenty years of longitudinal microdata on Kenyan individuals and a "mover" design. Controlling for individual fixed effects, urban migrants self-report better health and substantially lower incidence of fever, both for themselves and their children. These gains are not offset by increases in cough, diarrhea, or depressive symptoms, despite concerns about pollution, poor sanitation, and social isolation in growing African cities. Urban migrants also report increased healthcare expenditures, consistent with greater accessibility of care. Finally, they gain substantial weight, with corresponding increases in spending on protein, vitamin, and calorie-rich items such as dairy, fruits and vegetables, and processed foods. Overall, these results suggest that Africa's "urban health advantage" may at least partially reflect place effects, rather than selection of healthy individuals into migration.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the conditions under which intellectual property licensing relationships invert. Specifically, it examines when the operational value of the licensee's product demonstrably surpasses the symbolic value of the licensor's brand. Employing a qualitative case analysis methodology, the paper examines three primary cases: the three-decade partnership between Electronic Arts and FIFA, the content licensing arrangement between Disney and Netflix, and Sony's first-party IP ownership model as a structural counterexample. The central argument, termed the inversion thesis, proposes that licensing relationships are not static assets but dynamic structures in which bargaining power migrates from licensor to licensee as the licensee's operational ecosystem matures. The paper further demonstrates that standard mergers and acquisitions due diligence frameworks are structurally ill-equipped to capture this migration of value, and proposes a supplementary four-part evaluative framework covering revenue dependency, contract renewal risk, leverage dynamics, and asset infrastructure durability. The practical implication is direct: for acquirers and investors evaluating licence-dependent assets, the operative question is not whether the licence is legally valid, but whether the value resides in the licence itself or in everything built beneath it.

detail.abstract: The emergence of agentic AI is shifting online shopping from passive search and recommendation toward autonomous buying agents that monitor markets, reason about uncertainty, and make purchase decisions on behalf of consumers. We study the design of strategic buying agents that decide when to purchase an item within a finite shopping window. The central challenge is to translate price observations, the shopping window, and information about future price changes into a purchase-timing rule. We formulate this problem across a hierarchy of informational environments. In a stationary environment, prices are assumed to adjusted following an exogenously given Poisson price, and refreshed prices are drawn from a stable distribution; the optimal policy is a dynamic purchase threshold characterized by an ordinary differential equation. In a Bayesian learning environment, the price update rate is assumed to be known, but the price adjustment distribution is uncertain; the optimal rule remains threshold-based, with the threshold depending on posterior beliefs. We also bound the value of knowing the true price adjustment distribution. In a model-free robust environment, the agent relies only on price bounds and seeks worst-case protection; randomized static thresholds yield sharp guarantees for both competitive ratios and minimax regret. Finally, using Keepatracked Amazon product price histories of 367 items and 48,933 time-stamped posted-price observations, we evaluate our three policies and examine how they can be incorporated in language-model buying agents. The results show that these policies are competitive on the test instances and suggest that language models are more effective when used to select a policy and calibrate inputs than when used to make buy-or-wait decisions directly.

title: Hybrid Access in the Panama Canal: Equilibrium, Welfare, and Distributional Effects
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, Tsinghua University, Tsinghua University and University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

detail.title: Hybrid Access in the Panama Canal: Equilibrium, Welfare, and Distributional Effects
detail.abstract: Motivated by the Panama Canal's recent operational crisis, this paper investigates the strategic and welfare implications of allocating scarce public infrastructure capacity through a tripartite hybrid mechanism: advance booking, same-day priority auctions, and a regular first-come-first-served queue. We conceptualize this complex access architecture as a dynamic stochastic game, capturing heterogeneous users' intertemporal decisions under congestion uncertainty via a Markov Perfect Equilibrium (MPE) framework. To overcome the state space explosion induced by random daily demands, we introduce a first-order mixture distribution approximation that elegantly decouples macroscopic queueing evolution from microscopic valuation realizations. This structural reduction enables a new Virtual Curve Tangency algorithm, mathematically guaranteeing the existence and global uniqueness of the MPE. Our analysis identifies a form of market segmentation in which very high-valuation users may bypass advance booking and instead participate in the spot auction. We find that, while the auction can help mitigate severe system delays under extreme congestion, it also leads to a redistribution of surplus across users. In particular, it strictly shrinks aggregate canal demand and imposes severe congestion externalities on mid-tier vessels to finance a structural speed subsidy for vessels in the extreme upper tail.

detail.title: Strategic Market Entry Plan for Rasuwa Water: Positioning a Premium Himalayan Bottled Water Brand in Delhi, India
detail.abstract: The report is based on the analysis of the feasibility and strategic fit of Rasuwa Water entering the premium bottled water market in Delhi which suggests evidence-based market entry and positioning strategy. It combines secondary industry analysis and primary consumer research in evaluating the macro environmental conditions, industry structure, intensity of competition, regulatory environment and customer willingness-to-pay. In Delhi premium bottled water segment, economic attractiveness, regulatory barriers, competitive rivalry, buyer power and substitution threat were explored using a PESTLE and Porters Five Forces model. A structured consumer survey was used to gather primary data on the analysis of perceptions of safety, trust, lifestyle value, Himalayan origin symbolism, price acceptance and purchase intention. The results show that Delhi has significant demand potential because of high purchasing power, premiumization of consumption and favorable consumer associations with Himalayan origin and product safety. But the market also has intense competition, channel power as well as strict regulatory controls which demand clear differentiation, credible certification and targeted distribution. The consumer data verify that the premium bottled water is both a health product and a lifestyle brand and that willingness-to-pay in the mid-premium price is limited yet feasible. The study draws conclusion that the true Himalayan origin, quality assurance, and sustainability positioning of Rasuwa Water resonate well with the expectations of Delhi consumers. However, the company can only enter effectively by engaging in disciplined and focused pricing, trust signalling, and channel strategy. The report offers strategic recommendations on positioning, pricing, distribution and brand communication to help in a gradual, low risk, differentiationbased market entry strategy in the premium bottled water market in Delhi.

title: Burn Less, Earn More: Carbon Credit-Based Incentives for Sustainable Crop Residue Management
affiliations: Santa Clara University - Information Systems and Analytics, Eli Broad College of Business, Michigan State University, Indian Institute of Management (IIMB), Bangalore and Michigan State University - Department of Marketing and Supply Chain Management

detail.title: Burn Less, Earn More: Carbon Credit-Based Incentives for Sustainable Crop Residue Management
detail.abstract: Crop-residue burning (CRB) is a major source of air pollution and adverse health outcomes in developing economies. Although sustainable residue-management technologies exist, adoption is constrained by limited machinery capacity, coordination friction between farmers, and premature burning. We study the problem of an NGO that aims to maximize unburnt acreage in a village with one representative large farmer and one representative small farmer. The NGO must allocate its limited budget between procuring residue-management machinery and reducing the small farmer's premature burning behavior. The NGO can also obtain carbon credits for unburnt land, which can be used to design incentive policies to mitigate CRB. Methodology/Results: Based on discussions with practitioners*, we develop a game-theoretic model to analyze how the NGO should allocate its budget, and whether carbon credits obtained for unburnt land can reduce CRB. Using our baseline model, we characterize how the NGO should optimally allocate its budget to machinery procurement and behavioral interventions. We then study an individual credits policy under which each farmer receives credits proportional to their unburnt land. We show that this policy can be ineffective because individual credits do not resolve the coordination friction arising from asymmetric control over machinery access. We propose a collective credits policy that resolves this friction by connecting part of the farmers' incentives to village-level outcomes, leading to a significant decrease in CRB. Managerial Implications: Our results show that policies linking incentives across farmers can mitigate premature burning, improve machinery utilization, and expand unburnt acreage under budget constraints. The impact of such policies is significant when the cost of educating farmers to prevent premature burning is high. More broadly, our findings indicate that in social-sector operations with limited capacity and asymmetric control, incentive design based on collective outcomes can induce system-wide coordination and improve outcomes.

title: Universal Platforms, Unequal Access: Public Digital Health Initiatives in Developing Economies
affiliations: Florida State University - College of Business, University of South Carolina, University of South Carolina - Department of Management Science, Darla Moore School of Business, University of South Carolina and University of South Carolina

detail.title: Universal Platforms, Unequal Access: Public Digital Health Initiatives in Developing Economies
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Developing economies face significant challenges in distributing scarce resources to ensure equitable population healthcare access. Digital health initiatives are often promoted by policymakers and NGOs as a way to improve healthcare access, yet evidence regarding their efficacy in resource-constrained environments remains mixed. We examine how the rollout of a public digital health ecosystem impacts access to care, using the launch of India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) program. We then explore whether this impact is distributed equitably between groups. 

Methodology/results: Using a single-difference approach, we find that, after ABDM was fully launched in September 2021, monthly outpatient care volume increased by 22.9%. Further, a continuous difference-in-differences analysis examining the role of regional wealth in shaping the initiative's effectiveness indicates that wealthier sub-districts experienced larger increases in care volume than poorer regions. This gap in healthcare access after the initiative remains robust to alternative model specifications, alternate measures of wealth, aggregation across specific types of care, a falsification test, and the removal of outlier sub-districts. Finally, we investigate how this gap can be mitigated through infrastructure investments. We find that the gap in healthcare access after the initiative is lower in sub-districts with higher information access, physical infrastructure, and social support capacity. 

Managerial implications: This work provides evidence that implementing public digital health ecosystems can be effective in impacting the healthcare access of the general populace. However, our findings also highlight these access improvements can be distributed unequally between wealthy and poor regions. For policymakers and NGOs, our paper shows that digital health initiatives can systemically impact access to care, but proper considerations towards improving localized and allied infrastructure should be made to ensure equitable impacts for disadvantaged groups.

detail.abstract: We develop a continuous‑time principal‑agent model of private equity contracting that integrates ex‑ante screening and ex‑post monitoring under Brownian noise. The optimal screening‑only contract employs performance‑vesting bonuses triggered when cumulative output first hits an exponentially rising threshold. First‑best efficiency obtains when discount rates align, notwithstanding hidden effort. Under dual moral hazard, monitoring incentives asymmetrically reinforce screening, but not vice versa. Monitoring necessitates equity retention and a time‑varying payout boundary, thereby endogenously crowding out screening effort. The model rationalizes hurdle rates, catch‑up provisions, and valuation‑adjustment clauses, and informs the design of secondary funds and the resolution of exit liquidity frictions.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation has fundamentally reshaped modern business ecosystems, creating new opportunities and challenges at the intersection of industrial and commercial management. This paper presents a systematic review of the literature examining how digital technologies-including artificial intelligence, blockchain, and the Internet of Things (IoT)-influence supply chain performance from both operational and market-oriented perspectives. By integrating frameworks from industrial management (efficiency, optimization, and process control) with commercial management (customer behavior, market responsiveness, and value creation), a conceptual model is proposed to bridge the gap between production-side and demand-side dynamics. Findings suggest that organizations adopting an integrated digital strategy achieve superior supply chain agility, cost reduction, and customer satisfaction simultaneously. This study contributes to the emerging literature on cross-disciplinary management and offers practical implications for managers navigating digital disruption in competitive markets.

title: The Semi-Permeable Self: Osmotic Transformation and the Pursuit of Sarthakta

detail.title: The Semi-Permeable Self: Osmotic Transformation and the Pursuit of Sarthakta
detail.abstract: This study investigates the paradox of highly successful Indian professionals who choose to dismantle established careers despite achieving every external marker of institutional success. While classical Transformative Learning theory often identifies a singular "disorienting dilemma" as the catalyst for change, this research theorizes an alternative mechanism: Osmosis. Drawing on 25 long-form narrative performances from a career-transition podcast, the study applies Hoggan's (2016) metatheory to explore how transformation emerges through the slow, bidirectional saturation of a "semi-permeable self" by new environmental signals. The findings indicate that for this cohort, the primary center of gravity for change is axiological reordering. These professionals navigate a shift from "Socialized Success" towards Sarthakta, a culturally grounded concept of holistic meaning, autonomy, and relational legacy. Unlike Western individualist models of authenticity, this transformation is deeply relational, requiring a renegotiation of obligations to family and community. Furthermore, the study frames these retrospective accounts as "biographical repairs," where the act of narrative performance serves to bridge the gap between a former corporate identity and an emergent self. By introducing the concepts of osmotic absorption and axiological primacy, this research extends transformative learning scholarship into non-Western, high-stakes professional contexts, offering a more nuanced understanding of how whole-person change unfolds in the absence of acute crisis.

detail.abstract: This study reconceptualises sustainability in peer-to-peer accommodation (P2PA) as a multilevel, practice-based and institutionally embedded process. Existing research has largely adopted consumer-centric and macro-level perspectives, overlooking how sustainability is enacted through everyday hosting practices. Drawing on Social Practice Theory and an institutional perspective, this study conducts a systematic literature review to examine how host sustainability practices are formed, enacted, and transformed. The findings show that sustainability emerges through the dynamic configuration of three interdependent elements-meanings, competences, and materialsrather than from individual attitudes alone. Meanings, rooted in host identity and lifestyle orientations, shape how sustainability is interpreted; competences, developed through learning and social interaction, enable its enactment; and materials, including resource conditions and platform infrastructures, define its feasibility within institutional contexts. The study further demonstrates that sustainability practices are selectively enacted through processes of negotiation and adjustment, reflecting the alignment-or misalignment-of practice elements under structural constraints. Importantly, outcomes such as economic performance, guest experience, and social impact feed back into practice formation, highlighting the recursive and processual nature of sustainability. By advancing a practice-based and institutionally embedded framework, this study makes three key contributions: it shifts sustainability from an attitudinal to a configurational construct; explains the intention-practice gap as a problem of value-practice misalignment; and develops a relational, multi-level understanding of sustainability as co-produced across hosts, platforms, and broader institutional contexts.

detail.title: Tour-based Network Design and Demand Forecasting for Urban Air Mobility (UAM)
detail.abstract: Urban Air Mobility (UAM) has emerged as a promising alternative mode of urban transportation, offering the ability to bypass roadway congestion with environmentally friendly, safe, quiet, and on-demand eVTOL fleet. Our research focuses on estimating UAM demand and identifying key influencing factors using a tour-based demand model, which provides a more realistic representation of urban travel behavior. Compared with traditional trip-based models, the tour-based approach captures the interdependence of trips within a tour, thereby improving forecast accuracy for multimodal systems that integrate UAM. We apply Integer Programming (IP) to design the UAM network and estimate shifted demand, optimizing to minimize travelers' generalized costs. By modeling complete tours rather than isolated trips, the framework better reflects actual travel choices and mode-shift potential. Methodologically, building on Wu & Zhang (2021), we extended the single-allocation p-hub median problem to support a case study in the Tampa Bay Area. Results indicate that with 10 to 100 vertiports, 320 and 2,341 daily tours shift to UAM among the candidate tours. Travelers exhibit strong preferences for shorter access and egress times and distances. With the tourbased (round-trip) structure, personal vehicles (PVs) are primarily used to access and egress origin vertiports, whereas for-hire services are more commonly used at destination vertiports. Overall, the findings provide valuable insights for both city planners and UAM service providers, underscoring that UAM's success hinges on strategically located vertiports that enhance accessibility. The study highlights the importance of comprehensive, system-level planning to develop an efficient and competitive UAM transportation network.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the impact of the special recruitment of translators and translator-interpreters in Cameroon's public service between 2019 and 2024. A structured questionnaire was administered to 44 professionals to assess the perceived value of translation after recruitment, the clarity of translators' professional missions, and the opportunities and challenges encountered. The results indicate a generally positive perception of the initiative, with 66% of respondents reporting improved visibility and recognition of translators in public institutions, largely due to increased bilingual government communication. However, some respondents observed minimal change because of administrative inefficiencies and limited understanding of translators' roles. Job assignment remains problematic, as only 34% frequently receive tasks related to their training, while some receive no tasks. Professional development is also limited, with 80% reporting no training since recruitment. Other challenges include inadequate tools, poor working conditions, and limited career advancement. The study recommends clearer role definition, continuous training, improved working conditions, and stronger institutional recognition to enhance the effectiveness of translators in the public sector.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the influence of the Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) on the adoption of freight forwarding systems among companies in Parañaque City, Philippines. It specifically determines how DOI attributes such as relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability affect perceptions of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, and how these perceptions shape behavioral intention to use the system. Using a descriptive-correlational design, data were collected from 132 accredited freight forwarding companies through a validated survey instrument. Statistical analyses, including regression and ANOVA. Results revealed that relative advantage, complexity, trialability, and observability significantly influence perceived ease of use, while relative advantage, complexity, and observability strongly affect perceived usefulness. Furthermore, perceived ease of use significantly predicts behavioral intention, with perceived usefulness mediating this relationship. Findings also indicate that organizational maturity and financial capacity enhance readiness for digital adoption, while company size shows no significant effect. The study concludes that improving usability, demonstrating observable benefits, and offering pilot programs are critical strategies for successful system integration. These insights provide a framework for promoting digital transformation and sustainability in the Philippine freight forwarding sector.

detail.abstract: We study the long-run consequences of a large-scale branded product recalls for market demand and preference for private labels. Using the 2009-2012 recalls of Tylenol, the dominant brand of acetaminophen, as a natural experiment, we analyze weekly storelevel scanner data covering over 26,000 U.S. retail establishments from 2008 to 2020. A simple cross-molecule comparison of acetaminophen and ibuprofen sales reveals a large post-recall rise in the private-label share of acetaminophen and a persistent decline in total acetaminophen sales, but conflates the recall with any concurrent force that differentially affects either analgesic at the molecule level. To isolate the recall's causal effect, we use cross-sectional variation in each store's pre-recall Tylenol brand dependence: stores where Tylenol commanded a larger share of acetaminophen sales before November 2009 faced a greater recall-induced disruption. Comparing high-to lowexposure stores within the same retail chain, we find a large and lasting shift toward private-label acetaminophen in high-exposure stores: demand diverted to store-brand alternatives during the shortage did not fully revert once Tylenol returned to shelves. The private-label shift extends to adjacent analgesic molecules at roughly one-seventh the magnitude, pointing to a modest spillover effect within the broader analgesic category. We also document a statistically significant reduction in total acetaminophen category demand that persists for nearly a decade before dissipating.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops an empirical-theory model to explain why similar mortality pressure, successional replacement shocks, or key-person exits produce different Expansion Force outcomes across organizations, institutional environments, and states. Paper I defines the mortality vulnerability of embodied cooperation, Cemb, and the theoretical boundary of externalized cooperation, Cext. This paper asks a narrower question: when mortality pressure occurs, why do some systems suffer organizational rupture, credit contraction, and declining Expansion Force, while others absorb the shock through externalized cooperation structures?

The paper expresses Expansion Force under mortality pressure as Et = Pt x Ch,t x Cext,t, where Pt denotes the material and life-bearing substrate, Ch,t denotes horizontal coordination capacity, and Cext,t denotes effective externalized cooperation capacity. This expression is not a structural estimation equation. It is a reduced-form theoretical representation of the complementarity among material capacity, contemporaneous coordination, and externalized cooperation across death.

The paper treats mortality pressure, Mt, as an empirical shock rather than as a subtractive term in the formula. Mt includes key-person death, impairment, successional replacement shocks, functional exit, population aging, and intergenerational turnover pressure. Its theoretical function is to test whether a system remains dependent on embodied cooperation or has formed effective externalized cooperation.

The empirical logic of the paper is the interaction between mortality pressure and externalized cooperation, M x Cext. If Cext is effective, mortality pressure should generate smaller losses in firm performance, investment, financing capacity, organizational survival, innovation, credit maturity, or growth resilience. If Cext is merely formal or low quality, institutional continuity may preserve rigidity, monopoly, privilege, or liability evasion rather than productive cooperation.

The paper proposes three testable propositions. First, systems with higher dependence on Cemb should experience a more pronounced decline in Expansion Force after mortality pressure. Second, systems with stronger Cext should experience weaker negative effects from mortality pressure. Third, institutional continuity is not equivalent to Expansion Force: only effective Cext can potentially increase Expansion Force. The contribution of this paper is to move Mortality Economics from theoretical boundary-setting to a testable empirical-theory mechanism, and to provide the interface for subsequent institutional mechanism analysis.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Lifecycle Medicare Public Option (LMPO), a federally administered, tiered public option framework designed to align healthcare financing with predictable lifecycle utilization patterns. The model expands Medicare-style coverage to adults ages 26–54 through four age-stratified tiers and lowers full Medicare eligibility to age 55. It integrates Universal Health Savings Accounts (UHSAs), hybrid fee-for-service and value-based reimbursement, regulated private participation through Medicare Lifecycle Advantage (MLA) plans, and an explicit benefit bundle for each tier. This paper also proposes along five dimensions: (1) a formal three-scenario fiscal framework replacing single-point estimates; (2) explicit benefit bundles defining each tier's covered services and cost-sharing rules; (3) a phased demonstration model anchored in a state-level pilot before national scale-up; (4) a governance chapter specifying institutional roles for eligibility, risk adjustment, auditing, and appeals; and (5) a comparative policy section addressing the most common objections — including "Why not just lower Medicare to 60?" and concerns about employer crowd-out. The proposal's central claim is not that prevention saves money in the near term, but that lifecycle-aligned preventive investment can moderate the trajectory of late-life expenditure growth, improve population health value, and reduce avoidable catastrophic utilization.

title: Advancing Energy and Educational Equity in a Last-mile Andean Community

detail.title: Advancing Energy and Educational Equity in a Last-mile Andean Community
detail.abstract:
Remote Andean communities face persistent barriers to modern energy access and digital connectivity that limit instructional time, teaching practice, and student digital literacy. This case study documents a 2025 volunteer supported initiative led by Light Up the World with SAIT and NAIT to provide an integrated energy and connectivity solution for a high altitude public school in Huarcaya, Peru. A community engaged approach guided load assessment, system sizing, and installation planning. The deployment included an eighteen module 6.66 kW solar array, a 15 kWh lithium ion storage bank, three phase distribution to reduce voltage drop across dispersed buildings, campus wide LED lighting, a revitalized computer laboratory, and satellite internet backhaul. Commissioning confirmed electrical safety, load balancing, and network performance; early operation validated through onsite checks and online monitoring.

The integrated system enabled reliable daytime power, safe evening lighting, and meaningful connectivity, allowing teachers to prepare digital lessons, use multimedia instruction, and reinstate computing activities. Community members also gained new access options and modest income through a voucher based model. For volunteers, most of whom were first year students, the high altitude environment and demanding field logistics provided an authentic experiential learning context. Twelve week post return reflections demonstrated particularly high levels of teamwork, resilience, cultural empathy, identity development, and global citizenship, with strong meta cognitive awareness captured through rubric based assessments. These outcomes align with Kolb’s experiential learning cycle and underscore the value of structured pre departure preparation, on site mentorship, and delayed guided reflection. Integrating off grid solar, inclusive digital infrastructure, ethical partnership, and experiential education improved energy access and instructional capacity in a last mile setting and offers a replicable model for remote regions with strong solar resource, committed community participation, and adaptable storage pathways.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a classification gap in the public record of early-stage venture failure. Across 2,715 documented startup deaths assembled from six public datasets, representing approximately USD 660 billion in disclosed capital, only one record explicitly identifies buyer precision failure — the failure to name a specific reachable buyer with a defined trigger event and budget cycle — as the primary cause of death. This single-record figure should not be read as a count of how often buyer precision failure occurs in the underlying population of failures. It should be read as a count of how often the failure is named on the headstone. The paper proposes a six-stage framework for classifying commercial failure in early-stage ventures. The six stages — True Validation, Buyer Precision, Revenue Funnel, Buyer + Offer, Market + Funnel, and Commercial Decision — are defined operationally and applied to the master dataset. The paper defines the Stage 2 (Buyer Precision) failure mode in detail, and presents evidence — through dataset analysis and named case vignettes — that Stage 2 failures are systematically absorbed into adjacent labels in public post-mortem data, most often "no market need" (a Stage 1 label) and "bad marketing" or "bad distribution" (Stage 4 and Stage 5 labels). The paper is positioned as exploratory taxonomic analysis rather than confirmatory empirical research, and the limitations of the underlying methodology are documented openly. The intended contribution is a vocabulary correction: a category for a failure mode that occurs frequently in observed startup deaths but appears almost never in the taxonomies used to describe them.

title: Adopters as Bayesian Explorers: A Unified Model for Innovation Diffusion Dynamics
