detail.title: Adopters as Bayesian Explorers: A Unified Model for Innovation Diffusion Dynamics
detail.abstract: Despite decades of research into how new technologies and ideas permeate society, the field remains fragmented, lacking a unified framework to reconcile individual adoption behaviors with macro-scale diffusion dynamics. To address this gap, we introduce the Bayesian Exploration Adoption Model (BEAM), which conceptualizes potential adopters as boundedly rational agents operating under informational and cognitive constraints. Within this model, agents function simultaneously as active information seekers, passive receivers, and cognitive processors. We demonstrate that both classical and non-classical diffusion patterns-including standard S-shaped curves, simple and complex contagions, and the adoption "chasm"-emerge naturally from BEAM through parameter variation, without relying on phenomenon-specific, top-down assumptions. Furthermore, the model's high extensibility facilitates the disentanglement of two frequently confounded mechanisms: the network effect (the objective improvement of the new technology) and the peer effect (the subjective enhancement of its perceived value through social learning). We further demonstrate that these mechanisms can interact synergistically, complicating identification in observational data. Overall, BEAM provides a unified foundation for studying diverse innovation-diffusion dynamics and for evaluating the impacts and synergies of interventions that target distinct adoption bottlenecks, from information campaigns to financial incentives.

title: The Strategic Secretary Problem
affiliations: and National University of Singapore

detail.title: The Strategic Secretary Problem
detail.abstract: In the classic secretary problem, secretaries have no decision-making agency and are assumed to arrive in a random order. Motivated by modern online labor platforms, we consider a novel variant in which secretaries are strategic agents who choose their arrival times after privately observing their own quality scores. We model the interaction between a hiring firm and N + 1 strategic secretaries as a game and characterize the structure of its equilibria. This paper addresses two main questions. First, how do strategic secretaries choose their arrival times in equilibrium? Second, does granting secretaries strategic agency improve or reduce the firm's ability to select the best candidate? We show that when the firm can commit to a hiring policy and observe secretaries' quality scores, strategic behavior can improve the firm's probability of hiring the best secretary to approximately 0.71, compared with 0.58 in the classic problem. However, when the firm cannot commit ex ante, or when the firm observes only rank-based information about applicants, the probability of hiring the best secretary under strategic arrival is the same as in the classic problem. Our analysis highlights that granting applicants greater strategic agency can improve hiring outcomes, but only when accompanied by appropriate institutional conditions. In particular, firms should strengthen their ability to commit to hiring policies and prioritize access to more accurate quality signals.

detail.abstract: The assumption that the value of unsold goods at the end of a demand period is constant is widespread in inventory theory. It is common, for example, to assume that a fashion product can be liquidated at a constant salvage value if still in inventory when the demand period has ended. We show that, under general mathematical conditions, this modeling assumption will cause companies to underestimate both the value of lead-time reduction and the cost of lead time increases. Assuming a constant residual value in an environment where salvage values are allowed to depend on the amount of overage will systematically bias the value of lead time negatively.

detail.abstract:
Background: Decarbonisation of healthcare is a strategic priority in the UK, yet little is known about the system-level mechanisms that enable sustainability initiatives to become embedded within non-hospital settings. This paper reports the integrative synthesis from the GPNET-0 study, explaining how decarbonisation actions are mobilised, sustained, or displaced in general practice.

Methods: We conducted a theory-informed synthesis across qualitative, survey, and economic strands of a multi-level mixed-methods study.  A structured analytic matrix was used to integrate 174 discrete findings.  Realist logic guided development of explanatory configurations linking institutional conditions, organisational processes, and implementation outcomes.  Configurations were refined into programme theory testable statements. 

Findings: Across 17 explanatory configurations, decarbonisation was shaped less by individual attitudes than by interacting structural mechanisms.  Three mechanisms consistently underpinned implementation: legitimacy (clear policy signals and leadership endorsement), system-level alignment (coherence between national, regional, and practice-level governance), and workability (integration under constrained capacity).  Actions framed as discretionary, champion-led, or additive to existing workload were repeatedly displaced.  By contrast, initiatives embedded within governance expectations and aligned with routine practice processes were more likely to be sustained and normalised.

Interpretation: Decarbonisation in general practice is not primarily a behavioural challenge, but a structural implementation problem. Sustained change depends on institutional embedding, governance, coherence, and operational feasibility within everyday practice environments.  The programme theory presented here provides a system-level explanatory framework to inform future implementation strategies and empirical testing in general practice.

detail.title: Language, Power and Regional Recognition: Ashutosh Mukhopadhyay, the University of Calcutta and the Campaign for Vernacular Higher Education in Colonial India
detail.abstract: Between 1906 and 1923, Ashutosh Mukhopadhyay served five terms as Vice-Chancellor of the University of Calcutta, using those years to achieve what earlier generations had failed to accomplish: the sustained institutional recognition of Bengali, Assamese, Odia and Urdu across every level of the university curriculum, from matriculation to the postgraduate degree. Drawing on convocation addresses, commission reports and contemporaneous biographical accounts, this article argues that Mukhopadhyay’s campaign constituted a deliberate form of cultural nationalism pursued not through confrontation but through institutional strategy. The article situates this campaign against the progressive exclusion of modern Indian languages from the curriculum after 1868, the resistance of the colonial establishment, and the strategic use of the Raleigh Commission (1902) and University Act of 1904. Particular attention is given to the Assamese case and the commissioning of the Anthology of Assamese Literature (Axomiya Sahityar Xaneki), whose significance for the historiography of Indian language rights and regional cultural identity has not previously been assessed for an international readership. The article introduces the concept of institutional nationalism — the pursuit of nationalist cultural objectives through patient reform of inherited colonial structures — as an analytical frame for understanding Mukhopadhyay’s approach, and concludes that his multilingual educational vision anticipated the constitutional and institutional settlements of independent India in ways existing scholarship has not adequately recognised. In tracing this history, the article speaks to questions that remain unresolved across South Asia: who decides which languages belong in a university, and by what institutional means can that decision be contested and changed.

detail.abstract:
Scaling up effective policies often requires the attention of frontline bureaucrats with many competing responsibilities. Even when policymakers adopt effective programs, implementation may not follow. In a nationwide experiment in the Dominican Republic, we test interventions to increase school principals' implementation of an educational program proven effective in a previous RCT. Only 37% of control schools verifiably implemented the intervention when ordered to by the Ministry of Education, compared with 83% in the original trial. Implementation was no higher among schools that previously implemented the program in the RCT, suggesting that fixed costs of adoption do not explain non-adoption. We find precise null effects of sharing research evidence, providing modest financial incentives, or offering implementation assistance to principals. In contrast, additional reminder calls increased implementation by 20 percentage points. A second experiment targeting a different mandated program yields the same pattern: reminders produce large effects, while monitoring messages have smaller effects. Our findings point to limited attention among bureaucrats as an important barrier to scaling policies.
